### EDITOR'S INTRODUCTION

Jonathan Edwards' *A History of the Work of Redemption* stands apart in the body of his writings. We know that he intended to bring his thought to its summation in a volume which would give theology a new basis in the theme of God's redemption of the world. But the book assumed to be that volume was published in Edinburgh a decade and a half after his death and was a significantly edited transcription of a series of sermons he had preached in the late 1730s. Of all his major treatises, including *Religious Affections*, *Freedom of the Will*, and *Original Sin*, *Work of Redemption* alone was not delivered to the printer by Edwards himself. His other significant systematic works, the smaller essays known as the *Two Dissertations*, were nearing completion before his death. They were published within a decade, largely in the state in which he left them, under the supervision of his protégés. So the singularity of *A History of the Work of Redemption* begins with the fact that it was edited and published by an admirer removed in space and, to some degree, in time from its author.

The manner in which Edwards composed *Work of Redemption* is also noteworthy. The sermon series he delivered under this title was a quite extraordinary venture on his part; namely, the composition of an extended set of sermon-discourses based on one biblical text. The form was derived from that of the conventional Puritan plain-style sermon, and the series stretched out over the best part of six months. Certainly there are examples in the Edwards corpus of single sermons that required several occasions for delivery. There are also instances in which a series of sermons was grounded upon a single scriptural passage. Edwards developed one of these very shortly before he composed *Work of Redemption*. This series, known as "Charity and Its Fruits," presented a progressive analysis of the verses in St. Paul's Hymn to Love (1 Corinthians 13). But no extant series is like the

<!-- p. 002 -->

Redemption Discourse,[^002-note1] which sustained, or rather transformed, the structure of a single sermon across thirty separate preaching occasions. Although *Religious Affections*, Edwards' first great treatise, undoubtedly also originated in such a series, we do not have the manuscripts of the sermons, and the materials were thoroughly reworked for publication. So *Work of Redemption* is unique within the Edwards corpus with respect to the status of its text. No other uncompleted major treatise survives in such a "first draft."

*Work of Redemption* is unusual in other respects as well. Although Edwards conceived of it as a systematic discussion of the doctrine central to his mature thinking, he put the twelve manuscript booklets containing these sermons aside and as far as we can tell never preached the series or any part of it again. The only evidence that he began any significant revision is to be found in a notebook compiled toward the end of his life which probably marks the beginning of such a process. Thus both what was published as *A History of the Work of Redemption* and the original sermon-discourses on which it was based probably stand at some remove from what Edwards would have envisioned as its final, completed form. The fullest and most carefully wrought plan for the project on God's Work of Redemption occurs in his letter to the trustees of the College of New Jersey where, in discussing his reluctance to accept their invitation to become president of the college, he sketched an outline for the treatise.

In offering a new edition of *Work of Redemption*, the editor must proceed with caution and sensitivity. My introduction is divided into three parts. The first attends to the manuscript itself—its origin, characteristics, transmission, and eventual publication. In the second part I discuss the theological ideas which are at the heart of Edwards' endeavor, in particular the notion of the Work of Redemption as fundamental to the relationship between God and His creation. In doing so I deemphasize the importance conventionally given to the term *history* in the title, arguing instead that the work is primarily theological and that Edwards' use of the term is in that context. The third part describes how *Work of Redemption* was received upon its publication, how its influence spread, and how it has been reinterpreted as twentieth-century scholars have rediscovered in Edwards a major American thinker. The progression from text to doctrine and

<!-- p. 003 -->

finally to uses suggests the structure that is explicit in Edwards' sermons and that underlies his mature treatises.

### 1. The Redemption Discourse

#### The Setting Of The Redemption Discourse

By the spring of 1739, Jonathan Edwards had come into his own as successor to his grandfather, Solomon Stoddard, pastor of the church at Northampton in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Northampton was the most important settlement in the upper Connecticut River Valley, and as a consequence its church was extremely influential. The grandson had shown himself worthy to follow Stoddard by his role in the religious awakenings of 1734, which he chronicled in his *Faithful Narrative*.[^002-note2] This season of renewals made it evident that the impressive harvests of souls that had marked Stoddard's ministry were continuing after his death, under the stewardship of the grandson. In spite of rivalries and hard feelings, the succession was secure, and it was clear that Edwards would be a force to be reckoned with.[^002-note3]

Certain developments in the town of Northampton provided the occasion for the extraordinary preaching venture of the Redemption Discourse. In the course of the 1730s it had become increasingly evident that the town must replace its old meetinghouse with a new one, the third in its history.[^002-note4] Contemporary accounts show that a serious decision to build the new meetinghouse was made in the middle years of the decade.[^002-note5] While the new building was under construction, the gallery in the old one collapsed. No one was hurt, but this narrow escape from injury and death was taken as a sure sign that the townsfolk had acted wisely by committing themselves to building the new church. This more spacious meetinghouse also gave Edwards a larger stage on which to perform, to deliver (or "publish") his sermon-discourses—especially

<!-- p. 004 -->

after interest in religious affairs waned following the 1734 revival. It is noteworthy that he preached the extended series of sermons on 1 Corinthians 13, St. Paul's Hymn to Love, soon after the move to the new building.[^002-note6] The Redemption Discourse, which Edwards called "A History of the Work of Redemption," came a year later, preceded by four sermons on Genesis 3:11 preached in February 1739. That these ambitious sermon series closely followed the completion of the new structure was probably no accident.

The building of the new church was accompanied by an increasing differentiation of functions in the community. A new and separate town or county house was constructed soon after the new church,[^002-note7] physically segregating ecclesiastical from governmental functions for the first time in Northampton. This signals the maturation of the town as county seat and suggests its increased influence. Of course, separating government from religion threatened the tradition of ecclesiastical domination and helped create a situation in which it was ever more necessary for Edwards to assert the importance of religion. The Redemption Discourse exemplifies this important theme in Edwards' preaching.

By 1739 Edwards was secure as Stoddard's successor and had engineered and participated in the opening of a new ecclesiastical chapter in the life of Northampton, but he had also attracted wider attention by his publications. The first of these had been the "Publick Lecture" originally delivered in Boston on July 8, 1731, shortly after he had assumed the Northampton pastorate. "Published at the desire of several, Ministers and Others, in Boston who heard it," *God Glorified in the Work of Redemption* stands as an earnest of the central place that redemption would hold in his mature theological reflection.[^002-note8] Three years later (1734) he published another sermon, *A Divine and Supernatural Light*, *Immediately Imparted to the Soul by the Spirit of God*.[^002-note9] Soon thereafter *A Faithful Narrative* (1736) eclipsed these sermon-discourses at least in terms of public notice—it went through as many

<!-- p. 005 -->

as ten editions in a decade.[^002-note10] Edwards then prepared a set of additional discourses on five subjects (these were also originally sermons) for publication in 1738.[^002-note11] So by the time he turned his attention to composing the Redemption Discourse, he was well on the way to recognition both as an author and as a leader in New England ecclesiastical affairs.

This evidence for Edwards' growing stature is significant as background to the sermon series on God's Work of Redemption. It also seems clear that he was beginning to write sustained discourses of treatise length, although their initial—and perhaps only—"publication" might be from the pulpit. His 1738 sermon series is a quite remarkable descant on the text of 1 Corinthians 13. Technically the successive sermons of this series were preached on the verses in turn, so that Edwards was effectively appropriating an old and much-used device (expository preaching was thoroughly perfected in the Puritan tradition) in working through a biblical book (or even a series of books) over a long time. In this respect, then, he conceived the Redemption Discourse as a new and different kind of project, for it was based on a single verse of Scripture.

#### The Composition Of The Redemption Discourse

*A History of the Work of Redemption* originated as a series of thirty lecture-sermons that Edwards preached to the church in Northampton between March and August 1739. The collection of his manuscripts held in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale University includes the twelve booklets in which he wrote out these discourses. Like his other sermon booklets, they were designed to be held in the palm of his hand; each measures approximately 10.2 cm by 9.4 cm.

In general we know very little from either internal evidence or external testimony about the composition and delivery of these sermons.

<!-- p. 006 -->

Five of the thirty manuscript sermon units do contain notations, presumably concerning the time of their delivery. The first sermon was dated "March 1739," the tenth "April 1739," the sixteenth simply "June 17th," and the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth "August 1739." Beyond this, internal evidence makes it certain that at least the fourteenth and fifteenth, the eighteenth and nineteenth, and the twentieth and twenty-first sermons were composed and probably preached as linked pairs. In each case, the first unit of the pair (this possibly holds true for other sets as well) was intended for the forenoon and the second for the afternoon of the same day (undoubtedly Sundays). Otherwise the manuscript booklets do not indicate a specific day or time of preaching.

In the history of Edwards scholarship, more precise claims have been advanced about the preaching of this sermon series. Sereno Dwight, who was Jonathan Edwards' great-grandson and comprehensive editor and biographer, offered quite precise information about the distribution of the preaching occasions throughout this six-month period: "The eight first were delivered during that month [March], the eight next in the two following months, and the whole series, thirty in all, was completed before the close of August."[^002-note12] Dwight's statement is consistent with the internal evidence, and the distribution he sketched may have been based on inferences drawn from the texts. It is conceivable, of course, that Dwight had access to additional information about the series that is not currently available. He may also have compiled enough information about the delivery of other sermons to give him a basis for inferring the pattern of distribution he reports. In the course of this particular six-month period (March through August), Edwards' production of sermons other than those of the Redemption Discourse was markedly lower than usual. In tabulating extant sermons he presumably composed and delivered during 1739, we find that eight date from January and February, and thirteen from the months September through December. For March through August, there are only ten sermons independent of the thirty

<!-- p. 007 -->

of the Redemption Discourse.[^002-note13] This evidence does not necessarily support Dwight's claims about the *distribution* of the series across the months in question, but neither does it contradict his statement.

Dwight may also have been familiar enough with details of Edwards' activities and travels throughout this period to have made a good educated guess about when the sermons were preached. Ebenezer Parkman's *Diary* provides some information about Edwards' characteristic movements.[^002-note14] Parkman's relatively close observation of him in late May 1739 gives us grounds to suppose that the composition and delivery of the series caused no disruption of Edwards' normally demanding life. Parkman records that Edwards preached the public lecture in Boston (on the text 1 Timothy 2:5 [sic]) on May 24, a Thursday. On the next day Parkman dined with him at the Reverend Joshua Gee's in Boston, after which Edwards preached at "Elder Lymans." Whether he returned to Northampton on the Saturday is not certain, but it seems unlikely. On Sunday afternoon Parkman preached in his own pulpit at Westborough. (Westborough was only about a third the distance of Northampton from Boston.) On Monday afternoon (May 28) Parkman set off for Cambridge; when he returned he learned that Edwards had stayed at his home in Westborough that night. Probably Edwards was on his way to Northampton, although it is possible he was going back to Boston after having preached at Northampton on the twenty-seventh. From this we get a glimpse of the active life of a New England clergyman of the period; and we know that Edwards was, if anything, among the busiest. The larger point is that he composed and delivered the Redemption Discourse sermons during a time in which his schedule was already full. His normal Sunday sermons were the occasion of, and vehicle for, developing a series of lectures on this grand and encompassing theme.

Another of Dwight's assertions may also have come from internal evidence. He stated that Edwards "appears never to have repeated the Series of Discourses to his people."[^002-note15] This claim may rest on special information available to Dwight alone, but it is much more likely that he based it on his knowledge of Edwards' literary habits. When he

<!-- p. 008 -->

preached a sermon again Edwards usually noted the date; and he often thoroughly recast it.[^002-note16]

In the absence of more internal evidence we would ideally find external testimonies in, for instance, contemporary references to the actual delivery of this preaching series. As a hypothetical example, Joseph Bellamy, later to achieve prominence as an ecclesiastical leader, was apparently residing as a student in the Edwards household in this general period and might have heard these sermons. Our external evidence amounts to only one reminiscence, however, which was passed on to Edwards' grandson, Timothy Dwight, who cited it in *Travels in New England and New York*. Dwight devoted the fourth "letter" of his fourth volume to refuting an article in the *Edinburgh Review* which had claimed that "federal America" had "done nothing either to extend, diversify, or embellish the sphere of human knowledge." As a retort, Dwight argued that "the late President Edwards has more enlarged the science of theology than any divine of whom either England or Scotland can boast."[^002-note17] Furthermore, Dwight claimed that, save for Whitefield's, Edwards' preaching was unrivaled for eloquence. In this connection he introduced a reminiscence about the Redemption Discourse:

> The late Nehemiah Strong, Esq., a native of Northampton, and formerly professor of mathematics and natural philosophy in Yale College, observed to me that in early youth he heard Mr. Edwards deliver the sermons which now constitute the History of Redemption. His mind, he remarked, was from the beginning deeply interested in the subject. As it advanced, his feelings became more and more engaged. When Mr. Edwards came to a consideration of the final judgment, Mr. Strong said, his own mind was wrought up to such a pitch that he expected without one thought to the contrary the awful scene to be unfolded on that day and in that place. Accordingly, he waited with the deepest and the most solemn solicitude to hear the trumpet sound and the archangel call; to see the graves open, the dead arise, and the judge descend in the glory of his Father, with all his holy angels; and was deeply

<!-- p. 009 -->

  disappointed when the day terminated and left the world in its usual state of tranquility.[^002-note18]

Strong's testimony suggests that many *might* have remembered this significant series of lecture-sermons, but his is the only specific recollection. That Dwight published only this reference may mean that no contemporary written references to the series had survived even to his time.

From the outset Edwards clearly looked on the Redemption Discourse as an endeavor unlike any he had attempted before. First, all thirty sermons were organized around a single text: Isaiah 51:8, "For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation from generation to generation." The elaboration of the whole series is bounded by that text and the doctrine framed from it: "The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world." As in any Puritan sermon, there are entire sections which are "improvements" or "applications" for the benefit of Edwards' hearers. He concludes the series with a summary improvement. But a significant transmutation of the genre was taking place in spite of these and other formal elements and the constraints they placed upon the Redemption Discourse. The thirty edifying lectures had a narrative and theological unity so pervasive that, when they were finally published, their editor was able easily to strip away such sermonic characteristics as repetition of text and doctrine and reiteration of the argument. In so doing, he revealed the sustained treatise, organized by rationally ordered and largely chronological subdivisions, that we know as *A History of the Work of Redemption*.[^002-note19] This is one reason to think (in spite of his reference to the contrary in the well-known letter to the trustees of the College of New Jersey, see pp. 62–63 below) that, apparently from the point of their conception, Edwards intended to develop the Redemption Discourse sermons into a substantial treatise for publication.

Wilson Kimnach, a close student of the booklets in which Edwards wrote out his sermons, has suggested that, at least in certain cases, the division into "preaching units," that is, individual sermons, was arbitrary, or introduced only to permit Edwards to deliver the "treatise"

<!-- p. 010 -->

over thirty occasions.[^002-note20] In some places, the manuscript was clearly divided into sermons only after composition, but many of the sermons were composed with a view to being preached on a particular occasion.[^002-note21] Kimnach's larger point, however, is indisputable: the series is indeed a single, self-contained project. In this perspective, the development of a sermon series offered Edwards the opportunity to draft an initial version of a long-range undertaking; circumstances required its division into units that permitted delivery as sermons. Additional evidence that the Work of Redemption theme was fundamental to his mature thought appears in the "Miscellanies," that extraordinary series of essays recording the life of his mind from his college years on. There he repeatedly framed early entries around the theme of redemption and related subjects.[^002-note22] The Redemption Discourse summarized, as of the spring and summer months of 1739, Edwards' extensive reflections on the doctrine he believed to be most fundamental to Christianity.

There is no evidence that Edwards gave his attention to reworking (or, as noted above, repreaching) the series. There are, for example, no extensively redrafted sections.[^002-note23] In this connection, the circumstances of the time must be kept in mind. In little over a year after the conclusion of the series, George Whitefield made his first visit to New England, arriving at Northampton in the middle of October 1740. The extraordinary response to his preaching, and the itinerating which followed it, represent the social and cultural tumult later denominated the Great Awakening, in which Edwards became deeply involved. Under its influence, his intellect was increasingly devoted to developing a more discriminating understanding of the workings of the Spirit in human subjects. This preoccupation produced the extraordinary sequence of analytical studies of the phenomenon that began with his New Haven commencement sermon, "The Distinguishing Marks" (1741), progressed through *Some Thoughts Concerning*

<!-- p. 011 -->

the Revival

 (1742), and culminated in the magisterial treatise Religious Affections (1746).[^002-note24]

Religious Affections was itself, apparently, first worked out in the form of sermons.These publications of the early 1740s bear on the Redemption Discourse materials at most only indirectly, so that little, if any, discussion of them is appropriate. Edwards was so caught up by the Awakening and its demands that he had little opportunity, even if he had wished for it, to go back to revision and elaboration of the series of lecture-sermons about God's Work of Redemption. At the same time, there was a direct connection with the Awakening, for that revitalization of religious life concerned what we might term the subjective side of redemption, that is, its effect upon and appropriation by human subjects insofar as they were made participants in it. For our purposes, however, his publications of this period primarily demonstrate Edwards' proclivity to develop, and his manifest skill at transforming, essentially sermonic materials into sustained treatises. Thus the final form he seems to have intended for the Redemption Discourse was first perfected in the meticulous analysis of religious behavior and belief as they originated in the affections.

#### The "History" Project

A letter from the Scottish clergyman John Erskine to Joseph Bellamy, written on March 24, 1755, gives us some hint of Edwards' intentions for the Redemption Discourse. In passing Erskine writes, "Tho' I long to see Mr. Edwards' refutation of the several branches of Arminianism, yet I more long to see his intended history of man's Redemption. From such a pen upon such a subject, something highly valuable may be expected. May a kind providence preserve from danger a life so important."[^002-note25] Edwards had begun to exchange letters with Erskine in 1747. In the light of these comments we can safely surmise that he must have told Erskine something of his plans. But none of the letters he wrote to Erskine, at least among those that are preserved by Dwight in his *Life*, gives any details of what Erskine actually knew about the Redemption Discourse.[^002-note26] If Edwards' extensive correspondence

<!-- p. 012 -->

with Erskine survives, it has not been located and identified. What is clear, however, is that Erskine's special interest in the Redemption Discourse—an interest that eventually led him to edit it and arrange for its publication—antedated Edwards' death.

During the Stockbridge period (1750–57), Edwards began to turn his attention back to the Redemption Discourse. Three of his notebooks from this time establish, to greater and lesser degrees, that he was beginning to think about revising and reworking the lecture-sermons.[^002-note27] He seems to have pursued this enterprise most actively toward the end of the Stockbridge period, especially between 1755 and 1757. Elsewhere I have analyzed the contents of the three notebooks to see how they bear on Edwards' plans to work seriously on the project and have found strong evidence that in the later Stockbridge years he began in his usual fashion to approach the project systematically.[^002-note28] He seems to have thought that his knowledge of Christian history needed to be augmented, so he started to read comprehensively in the history of the early Western church, focusing his attention on the Roman popes. Concurrently, he made notes about important points other authors had made which bore on the Redemption project. Finally, in the most distinctive of the three notebooks, he jotted down thoughts about the form, the content, and the argument of the project concerned with the Work of Redemption, including variant titles and different patterns of organization. The specifics of these notebooks will be introduced later.[^002-note29] For the moment their relevance is that they corroborate the statements Edwards made about the Redemption project in his letter to the trustees of the College of New Jersey.

With the death of Aaron Burr, Edwards' son-in-law and the college's president, its fragile existence in New Jersey—it had but recently settled at Princeton—was once again threatened.[^002-note30] Edwards had links to the college from its early days. Indeed he seems increasingly to have felt such a kinship to the Middle Colony "New Side" Presbyterians

<!-- p. 013 -->

that it to some extent superseded his ties to the Connecticut Valley churches and the Awakeners in the Bay area. It is not surprising that the college's trustees turned to him as an obvious candidate for its presidency. In offering a dispassionate analysis of his strengths and shortcomings which stands as a model for candor on the part of presidential candidates, Edwards also reviewed the current projects he thought would necessarily be delayed or abandoned if he accepted the office. In this context he offered much the clearest statement that we have about his plans for the development and completion of the Redemption project, signaling that it was uppermost in his thoughts at that point. "I have had on my mind and heart, (which I long ago began, not with any view to publication,) a great work, which I call a *History of the Work of Redemption*, a body of divinity in an entire new method, being thrown into the form of a history."[^002-note31] So when Edwards moved from Stockbridge to Princeton in January 1758, he was again decisively deflected from the "history" project he considered a development of the Redemption Discourse of 1739. His death within two months (March 22, 1758) prevented him from ever returning to it.

#### The Redemption Discourse And The "Miscellanies"

One significant perspective upon the place of the Redemption Discourse in Edwards' intellectual life can be gained from his "Miscellanies."[^002-note32] To this point these have not been used to interpret the Redemption sermons, although Thomas Schafer's critical work on them has led to confident dating, at least of the periods in which individual entries were copied into the notebooks. It is not surprising that the "Miscellanies" contain traces or foreshadowings of the Redemption Discourse throughout, but their full exploitation in this respect must await their publication in the Yale critical edition. The suggestions that follow are, therefore, provisional and necessarily impressionistic.

There are at least three different respects in which the "Miscellanies" bear on the present inquiry. First, from the early entries, and continuing throughout the entire series of well over a thousand, the

<!-- p. 014 -->

theme of redemption as the greatest of God's works appears repeatedly. Second, two extended entries offer quite remarkable evidence that Edwards had reflected thoroughly on the themes that would define the outline of the project as a whole, perhaps as early as two to three years before he began to compose the sermons. Finally, a half-dozen or so entries, contemporaneous with or made shortly after the preaching series in 1739, include explicit references to the Redemption Discourse.

A very large proportion of the "Miscellanies" explicitly concern redemption. For example, No. 38 (probably summer 1723) is a brief discussion of the "Harmony of God's Attributes in the Work of Redemption." No. 60, titled "Hades" and written not long after, perhaps in the early fall of that year, is a discussion of the process of redemption with regard to both individuals and groups. No. 156, written when Edwards was a tutor at Yale, is devoted to the defeat of Satan and introduces themes that are developed at great length in the Redemption Discourse proper. Discussions introduced under topics as various as "New Earth," "Heaven," "Kingdom of Christ," "Hell" or "Hell's Torments," "Resurrection," "Covenants," and "Lord's Day," among many others, are directly relevant to the project. Many are even more explicit: "End of Creation," "Millennium," "Universal Redemption," "Incarnation," and, above all, "Work of Redemption."

These themes had been fully explored by Edwards before he preached the public lecture in Boston on July 8, 1731, that, when published, carried the title *God Glorified in the Work of Redemption*, *by the Greatness of Man's Dependence upon Him*, *in the whole of It*. They continue as subjects throughout the "Miscellanies" until the end of his life. Certain formulations gain preference during particular periods in the course of his entries in these notebooks. The "Wisdom of God in the Work of Redemption" became significant in the early 1730s (examples are Nos. 508, 510, 521, 524, 526, 554, 569, 604, 614, 616, 633, 653, 664, and 681). He continued to use this formulation throughout the Northampton years, although less frequently. With No. 802 he began to use the phrase "Progress of Redemption" as an inclusive designation (other examples are 814, 833, 834, 835, 907, and 932). This he emended to "Progress of the Work of Redemption" in the early 1740s (see Nos. 935, 946, 949, 952, and 991). To identify individual essay-entries in this fashion, however, may obscure their interconnection. Edwards weaves themes into and around the redemption motif so that, taken as a whole, the "Miscellanies"

<!-- p. 015 -->

dramatically confirm what he claims so explicitly, that this was *a*, if not *the*, central focal point of his theological reflection.

Beyond this, there is clear evidence in two entries that Edwards systematically brought together the basic themes of his sermon series at least two to three years before actually composing it in 1739. No. 702 (probably 1736 or 1737) is titled "Work of Creation. Providence. Redemption." It amounts to a lengthy argument (twenty-one pages in typescript) that the works of creation and providence are subservient to the Work of Redemption. Within this framework Edwards explored many of the theses and themes that concerned him throughout the sermons he preached on the Work of Redemption. In particular, he analyzed Adam as a type of Christ, and the relationship between creation by Christ and re-creation, or the new creation in him. The incarnation is central to this argument, as is the perfection of redemption in the end of the world. In many respects No. 702 is a précis of the argument of the Redemption Discourse.

This is made all the more evident by No. 710, an equally long entry, which stands as an appendix to No. 702. It explores the implications of viewing the internal transactions of the Trinity as the energizing force behind creation as well as redemption: "The world was created that Christ might obtain a spouse." This leads Edwards to explore the secondary roles of angels and men in these transactions. It also leads him to develop the theme that bulks so large in the sermons, the respects in which the devil and his Antichrist mirror God and his Christ. Edwards' typological analysis is very important to these sections. Taken together, these two miscellanies offer the earliest evidence of his intentions concerning the Redemption Discourse and show how thoroughly he developed his grand plan of the project some time before he actually wrote and preached the sermons.

Finally, several of the miscellanies give direct evidence that, probably shortly after preaching the sermon series, Edwards gave thought to its extension and specification at certain points. In the manuscript of the sermons, he directed himself to particular miscellanies at three separate places. These three are Nos. 802, 803, and 810, generally dated in mid- to late 1739, or roughly toward the end or at the conclusion of the period in which he delivered the Discourse.[^002-note33]

<!-- p. 016 -->

No. 802 is called "Progress of Redemption" and begins with directions: "Add this to Discourse on Isai 51.8. Sermon 18 at the end of the 2 particular under the 4. General Observation." In this miscellany Edwards develops the argument that Christ's spiritual "comings to judgment" as spoken of in Scripture anticipate what will be done "externally" at the day of judgment.

No. 803 is titled "Progress of Redemption. Christ's Coming to Judgment." Here the instruction is: "Join this to what is said concerning the state of things requiring Christ's coming to judgment at the time he will come in Discourse from Isai. 51.8. Sermon 28. The 3d particular concerning the last Apostasy." Its theme is that the greater light available to the wicked of the world at that point will make their apostasy the more heinous in God's sight. Therefore the destruction will be all the more terrible.

Finally, No. 810 is an addition to No. 359, which concerned the Scriptures in relation to redemption. No. 810 especially reflected on Job and why such a book was inserted in the canon. It seems less fully and directly linked to the Redemption Discourse than Nos. 802 and 803, but it does stand as further evidence, if such be needed, of Edwards' preoccupation with this theme at the end of the 1730s.

Two other brief adjacent essays, Nos. 806 and 807, directly relate to the Redemption Discourse. No. 807 is titled "Work of Redemption the Greatest of God's Works." It concerns the duration of the new creation (about six thousand years plus an additional thousand years in the millennium) in comparison with the old (six days plus a sabbath day). In this brief note Edwards explicitly refers to "Discourse on Isaiah 51:8 1 Inference at the close of Sermon 29." No. 806 is entitled "New Heavens and New Earth" and does not explicitly refer to the Redemption Discourse, although it directly concerns its overall theme.

From this brief consideration of the "Miscellanies," it should be clear that any future interpretation of the sermon series that formed the Redemption Discourse must include study of the large number of relevant entries in that remarkable series of notebooks. As much as anything else these essays, which Edwards compiled throughout his life, demonstrate how prolonged and deep was his commitment to develop a theology based upon the theme of the redemption of the world as a consequence of the internal dynamics of the Trinity—that is, the interrelationships of Father, Son, and Spirit.[^002-note34] By the same

<!-- p. 017 -->

token the Redemption Discourse stands as a systematic elaboration of a grand theme that appears at a remarkable number of places and times and under many different headings in the storehouse of his essays.

#### The Fate Of The Sermon Manuscripts

In moving to Princeton without his family (Sarah Edwards was to remain in Stockbridge with the children for a transitional period), Jonathan Edwards apparently entrusted the bulk of his manuscripts to Samuel Hopkins, protégé and then near neighbor in Great Barrington, Massachusetts. Writing on January 19, 1758, to Joseph Bellamy, another protégé and colleague then living in Bethlem, Connecticut, Hopkins reported that the preceding day Edwards had departed on the journey from Stockbridge to Princeton.[^002-note35] Most significantly, he reported that he had left "long papers" and manuscript sermons in his possession, permitting him to go through them and make use of them while they were in his care. In Edwards' Stockbridge years, Hopkins and Bellamy had frequent exchanges with him about their respective writings in progress. Thus many of Edwards' manuscripts were undoubtedly well known to Hopkins, and he would have been a trusted and obviously sympathetic custodian for them until in due course they could be moved to New Jersey. There is no reason to suppose that the sermon manuscripts of the Redemption Discourse were separated from the other manuscripts—for instance, making the journey to Princeton with their author. It is a conjecture, of course, but a reasonable one, that they did not remain with Sarah under these circumstances; presumably the works about which Edwards was most concerned were left with Hopkins.

Edwards died in a matter of weeks, on March 22, 1758. While technically Sarah was executor of his literary remains, and was succeeded in this task at her death by the eldest son, Timothy, the actual possession of (and responsibility for) the manuscripts seems to have rested in other hands, primarily those of Samuel Hopkins.[^002-note36] His role

<!-- p. 018 -->

as conservator lasted for the better part of a decade. In autobiographical reflections written years later and published in 1805, Hopkins reported his memory of the arrangements made for the manuscripts and papers during the years immediately following Edwards' death. "Upon the death of Mr. Edwards, Mrs. Edwards, in consequence of verbal directions given to her by Mr. Edwards in his life time, put all his manuscripts and his library into my hands, and care: His manuscripts to be disposed of by me, and two other ministers."[^002-note37] Joseph Bellamy was certainly one of the two other literary executors in this period; Gideon Hawley, another younger associate, may have been the third. There is significant correspondence between Hopkins and Bellamy in the ensuing years about these shared responsibilities.[^002-note38] Inferences drawn from these letters, as well as Hopkins' own assertions, make it evident that of the three he was the most thoroughly involved with the manuscripts.

> As these manuscripts were in my hands a number of years, I paid my chief attention to them, until I had read them all, which consisted of a great number of volumes, some of them large, besides sermons, of which sermons I did not read the whole. In doing this I had much pleasure and profit. My mind became more engaged in study, rising, great part of my time, at four o'clock in the morning to pursue my study, in which I took great pleasure.[^002-note39]

Others outside this circle, including John Erskine in Scotland, expressed an interest in Edwards' "literary remains." He wrote to Bellamy on June 8, 1759, with the thought that subscriptions could be obtained, presumably in Scotland, for two octavo volumes of "practical works."[^002-note40] He also requested a description or listing of the manuscripts, presumably with a view to selecting additional items and proposing them for publication. A Dissenting minister in Ipswich, England, Mr. Gordon, also expressed interest in abridging *Religious Affections* for the English market. Indeed, from a letter written a year later, it is apparent that he wanted to reissue Edwards' published writings, hoping to find a market for them through the London book-seller

<!-- p. 019 -->

Field.[^002-note41] Thus during the first years after Edwards' death, while legal title to the manuscripts remained with the family, actual work in and with them, not excluding developing plans for their publication, was very much in the hands of others. Only when Jonathan Edwards, Jr., had graduated from the College of New Jersey and was judged suitable, in part through residing in both the Hopkins and Bellamy households and pursuing theological studies under them, did the responsibility for his father's literary materials pass into his hands.[^002-note42] This development restored possession of and control over the corpus of manuscripts to the family, where it remained for more than a century.[^002-note43]

It is evident that Hopkins invested great energy in working with the manuscripts. By his own account, noted above, he worked through them with great love and benefit to himself. His access to them was made thoroughly secure as a consequence of Sarah Edwards' request that he write a memoir of her husband:

> And Mrs. Edwards solicited me to write the life of Mr. Edwards, to be published, with a number of sermons, to be selected from his manuscripts. I considered myself very unequal to writing his life; but as by having the possession of his manuscripts, I was under better advantage to do it, than others, I engaged to do the best I could; and if it should be approved of by a number of friendly, judicious ministers, I would consent to have it published, on condition that my name should not be put to it. Accordingly it was published with a number of posthumous sermons, most of which I transcribed myself from his manuscripts.[^002-note44]

<!-- p. 020 -->

Although Sarah died within six months of her husband, Hopkins respected her request and wrote the first substantial memoir of Edwards. His work has been basic to biographical study of Edwards ever since. But before *The Life and Character of the Late Reverend Mr. Jonathan Edwards* was published in 1765, including *Sermons on Various Important Subjects*,[^002-note45] Hopkins was more than a little frustrated by erstwhile collaborators. To Joseph Bellamy he wrote with apparent testiness on January 4, 1764: "I should be glad you would transcribe some of the sermons you mention without any *ifs or ands* [italics original]. I and my brother have transcribed 10 sermons, which I hope to send to Boston [to the publisher Kneeland] soon, but these with the life & the 6 Mr. Searl has transcribed, will not be enough to make one Vol."[^002-note46]

Apparently Hopkins and Bellamy also collaborated in issuing *Two Dissertations*[^002-note47] in the same year. The same letter requests Bellamy to "send me that on Virtue the first safe opportunity," because he is planning to go to Boston to prosecute the proposal.[^002-note48] Hopkins' letter also reports having finished transcribing the "Last End."[^002-note49] From this we can infer that it was Bellamy's transcription of "The Nature of True Virtue" that he asked for. In these efforts, Hopkins discharged his editorial labors in a conservative fashion, showing respect for the manuscript text and seeking to preserve it from excessive editorial intervention in a fashion less often followed by later editors.

#### The Publication Of The Redemption Discourse

At some point during this period, possibly during the winter of 1765 and the spring of 1766, Jonathan Edwards, Jr., took physical possession of the manuscripts. He also began to function as literary executor of his father's papers. Certainly by March of 1767, when he was a tutor at Princeton, Edwards, Jr., had replaced Hopkins (and Bellamy, and perhaps Hawley) as the agent responsible for them. At this point Bellamy, and probably Hopkins, too, effectively passed out of the picture. In the fragmentary materials which bear on the location and status of the Edwards materials in this initial period, no evidence has been found to suggest that serious and sustained attention

<!-- p. 021 -->

was ever given to the question of whether the Redemption Discourse should be transcribed and published. It is clear that the response to the proposals for publishing Edwards' works had been disappointing, at least on the western side of the Atlantic. Perhaps because of the lack of interest in the Colonies, Edwards, Jr., seems to have sought to capitalize on the rather livelier interest in his father's library remains in Scotland especially, but to some degree also in England. We have noted John Erskine's correspondence with Edwards (which Edwards valued so highly, particularly during the Stockbridge years when he was so physically isolated and Erskine sent him current books) as well as with Bellamy. Although we do not have direct evidence, it is most likely that Erskine now turned to the son, recently become literary executor, and urged upon him his own interest in seeing the Redemption Discourse published. In his "Preface" published in the first Edinburgh edition[^002-note50] and dated at New Haven on February 25, 1773, Jonathan Edwards, Jr., referred directly to Erskine as removing the obstacle presented by "the difficulty of getting any considerable work printed in this infant country hitherto." According to Edwards, Jr., Erskine "engaged a bookseller to undertake the work, and also signified his desire that these following discourses in particular might be made public."

The question of who transcribed the manuscripts that were published by John Erskine in Edinburgh in 1774 as *A History of the Work of Redemption* now becomes extremely important. If they were transcribed by Jonathan Edwards, Jr., there is no reason to suppose that Erskine, publisher of the first printed version and its avowed editor, ever saw the originals. Every subsequent edition would then have been based upon a printed version initially edited from a transcript, and not from the manuscripts themselves, with what loss of nuance and authenticity may be imagined.

First we must consider Erskine's possible role in the transcription. If he was responsible for encouraging and facilitating the publication of the sermon series on the Work of Redemption, did he also have a hand in transcribing them? From the fact that he unequivocally claims to have edited the sermons into the form of a treatise, it is possible to infer that he arranged to transcribe them. His advertisement permits this reading: "The manuscript being intrusted to my

<!-- p. 022 -->

care, I have not presumed to make any change in the sentiments or composition. I have, however, taken the liberty to reduce it from the form of sermons, which it originally bore, to that of a continued treatise; and I have so altered and diversified the marks of the several divisions and subdivisions, that each class of heads might be easily distinguished."[^002-note51] Dated April 29, 1774, some fourteen months after Jonathan Edwards, Jr.'s, preface, this advertisement might suggest that the transcription (as well as the editing) of the Redemption Discourse was accomplished in Scotland. But circumstantial evidence casts doubt upon this interpretation.

First, Jonathan Edwards, Jr., himself published a set of his father's sermons at the end of the decade. In the preface to the book *Sermons on the Following Subjects*, published at Hartford in 1780, he offered the following statement: "As to the sermons themselves, they were not transcribed with any view to a publication in this country. In the year 1773, I was desired by a gentleman in Scotland, to transcribe a number of the author's sermons on some of the most plain, practical and experimental subjects, that they might be printed there."[^002-note52] (This is dated December 21, 1779.) It is highly unlikely that different understandings and approaches to transcription, editing, and publication would govern these two ventures (the publication of *Work of Redemption* and *Sermons*) so closely related in kind, context, and time.

Second, Edwards, Jr.'s, reasons for selecting these particular sermons closely echo Erskine's grounds for recommending *A History of the Work of Redemption* to its potential readers: "Though the acute philosopher and deep divine appears in them, yet they are in the general better calculated for the instruction and improvement of ordinary Christians, than those of President Edwards's writings, where the abstruse nature of the subject, or the subtle objections of opposers of the truth, led him to more abstract and metaphysical reasonings."[^002-note53] Thus the parallel characterizations with regard to the *Sermons* Edwards, Jr., published in 1780 and the *Work of Redemption* Erskine published in 1774 suggest they were related projects produced by similar methods.

Comparable considerations apparently also led Erskine to publish Edwards' *Twenty Sermons* in Edinburgh in 1789, and a selection of his

<!-- p. 023 -->

*Miscellaneous Observations*, also in Edinburgh, in 1793.[^002-note54] The language of the prefaces to these works suggests that the same method of collaboration was used: Erskine took the initiative in soliciting Jonathan Edwards, Jr., to publish materials, but it was the latter who transcribed them and forwarded the transcriptions to Erskine.

Thus it is likely that this method was also used for the manuscript published as *A History of the Work of Redemption*. We can, then, reasonably surmise that while Erskine clearly exercised considerable initiative in *editing* the Redemption sermon materials into treatise form, it is almost certain that Jonathan Edwards, Jr., *transcribed* the booklets, providing the manuscript which Erskine used in preparing copy for the publisher.

This interpretation of the evidence is corroborated by charges leveled at Jonathan Edwards, Jr., some years later, when it came his turn to be separated from the church he served as pastor.[^002-note55] Roger Sherman, Connecticut judge, member of the Continental Congress, and signer of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, was a prominent (and dominant) figure in the White Haven church served by Edwards, Jr., although he was not close to its everyday life because of his frequent and prolonged absences from New Haven. When, in 1790, the proceedings which led to Edwards, Jr.'s, departure were under way between the pastor and his church, Sherman inquired of other members about the grounds for the dispute. David Austin, who was then emerging into prominence, offered the observation that Edwards, Jr., had devoted inordinate time to "business" affairs in his study: "has he not been imployed a great proportion of his time there in business of a pecuniary nature? has he not imployed himself in transcribing a volume of his father's sermons & printing them at Hartford? In transcribing the History of Redemption & preparing a copy to be printed in Scotland?" Sherman's response took the form of defending the appropriateness of these activities on the part of Jonathan Edwards, Jr. It did not challenge the essential correctness of Austin's description, nor did it question the accuracy of the assertion about Edwards, Jr.'s, role in transcribing the Redemption Discourse

<!-- p. 024 -->

course booklets.[^002-note56] This suggests that Edwards, Jr.'s, work as transcriber of his father's manuscripts was common knowledge among the son's associates.

This reconstruction of how the Redemption Discourse was transcribed and readied for publication has recently been confirmed by the discovery of evidence in Jonathan Edwards, Jr.'s, hand. In a letter dated April 28, 1792, Isaiah Thomas, who reprinted the Erskine edition of *A History of the Work of Redemption* at Worcester (1792), wrote to Edwards, Jr., expressing surprise that the son might have any legal claim to it. In drafting a rather irritated reply on the same sheet, the son presented the basis for his claim in the following language: "I was at the pains of transcribing and publishing that volume at a time when the laws of our country secured nothing to authors or proprietors of manuscripts." In his response Thomas rejected Edwards, Jr.'s, claim. Thus the son's role in transcribing the Redemption sermon series in New Haven during the early 1770s is clear. There is, further, a strong presumption for thinking that the original manuscript booklets never crossed the Atlantic and that their editor and publisher, John Erskine, worked solely from the son's transcription.[^002-note57]

In general the son was respectful of the integrity of his father's manuscripts, as Hopkins had been. Occasionally he undertook to rework some of Edwards' prose. This intervention was especially pronounced in the case of his transcriptions of some "Miscellaneous Observations." At a very few points his handwriting may also be identified in the Redemption booklets themselves.[^002-note58] It seems likely that Edwards, Jr., did not have a collaborator in the transcription of this series of sermons, although it is remotely conceivable that he made use of earlier drafts by Hopkins—and possibly others. The difficulty of Edwards' hand, the absence of a ready market for additional published materials by him, and the sheer length of the manuscripts, however, all make such collaboration or dependence improbable.

<!-- p. 025 -->

We have already noted that John Erskine's advertisement to his edition, dated Edinburgh, April 29, 1774, reports that the younger Edwards entrusted the manuscripts to him for editing. We return now to Erskine's treatment of the materials he was to publish as *A History of the Work of Redemption*. He clearly exercised the prerogative of editor in reducing the sermons to a coherent treatise. In this he followed the logical structure Edwards gave to the whole, dividing the Work of Redemption into three great periods, and further subdividing each of these either into relevant subperiods or according to analytic principles. (He used the analytic method especially with the middle period, comprising Jesus' life with its purchase of redemption, and in the projection of events that would complete the last period beyond Edwards' own time.) Erskine suppressed the marks of the preaching occasions, for example, the repetition of text and doctrine or recapitulation of the preceding sermon(s), which Edwards often provided. In doing so, he did readers a disservice, for these introductory sections were often preludes to Edwards' further development of his argument and had relevance to his thesis as well as some literary interest. On the other hand, Erskine did not delete such substantial sermon-derived sections as the improvement at the end of the first period (which comprised Sermon Thirteen) or the application at the end of the second period (in Sermon Seventeen)—and certainly not the application of the whole (which begins in Sermon Twenty-nine and takes up the whole of the concluding, and thirtieth, sermon).

At a less general level, presumably it was Jonathan Edwards, Jr., who exercised the prerogative of completing certain sections that his father had left as little more than outlines of his argument. Often this occurred when he was compiling scriptural warrants for a position or when he was developing an interpretation of a particular verse. Indeed, if we assume that the original manuscripts (Edwards' sermon booklets) remained with his son in New Haven, Erskine may never have known how relatively unfinished and incomplete some sections of the Redemption Discourse actually were. *A History of the Work of Redemption. Containing*, *The Outlines of a Body of Divinity*, *In a Method entirely new* was published in Edinburgh for W. Gray in 1774. There are no grounds to suppose that any subsequent version rested on additional study of the original manuscripts, or for that matter, on familiarity with Jonathan Edwards, Jr.'s, transcription of them.

<!-- p. 026 -->

#### The Published Versions Of A History Of The Work Of Redemption

John Erskine's 1774 edition of *A History of the Work of Redemption* has frequently been republished in English.[^002-note59] In 1782 it was reissued in Edinburgh and reprinted at Boston as well. It was first issued in New York in 1786. Before 1800 this same version was reprinted three more times in Edinburgh (1788, 1793, 1799), and also in Worcester, Massachusetts (1792). In addition, an augmented version, known as the "Pitcher edition" after its editor, George Pitcher, was brought out in London in 1788. This included historical, critical, and theological notes along with a section on "The Life and Experience of the Author." The Pitcher text has some minor variations from Erskine's, but there is no basis for supposing that it rested on a fresh transcription of the manuscripts or even reference to them or to Jonathan Edwards, Jr.'s, transcription. In all respects the Pitcher edition seems to derive from the Erskine text in an attempt to improve it. There is no possibility of independent reference to the original. The same applies to the Pitcher edition as brought out by Swords in New York in 1793. This later edition (Pitcher and then Swords as derived from it) suppresses Erskine's advertisement, offers a much fuller syllabus than Erskine's table of contents, appends extensive notes, and provides an index of references. But none of this elaborate paraphernalia derives from Edwards or has any basis in his manuscripts (sermon booklets or notebooks).

In general Pitcher's departures from the Erskine version take the form of occasionally eliminating a redundant sentence. A selective analysis of variations between these editions shows that the Erskine text is always fuller and always stands closer to the original manuscript. It is proof of the complete dependence of the Pitcher version on the Erskine version that it follows Erskine in sections of the text that Edwards, Jr. (or Erskine) undertook to complete or otherwise finish, sections left in rough form in Jonathan Edwards' preaching booklets. At most it could be claimed that Pitcher had access to the transcription that Erskine edited, but it is more reasonable to suppose that Pitcher's version derived wholly from Erskine's.

In addressing the issue of variations between the Erskine and Pitcher versions of the texts, the editor of the Worcester edition of

<!-- p. 027 -->

Edwards' *Works* explicitly chose to use Erskine's corrected 1793 text (the fourth Edinburgh edition).

> This [the 1793 text] is according to the form to which the manuscript was reduced by Dr. Erskine, and appears to have been printed with uncommon accuracy, probably under the eye of the Doctor. This is preferred to the London Edition, published in the year '88 by Mr. Pitcher. The Editor of this Edition [Pitcher], though he appears to have been conscientiously careful to preserve the sentiments of Mr. Edwards, has so varied the style, that we cease to rely that what we have is the composition of the original author.[^002-note60]

While this judgment about the relative merit of these versions is undoubtedly correct, the characterization of the Pitcher edition overstates its degree of independence from Erskine's edition, insofar as the author seems to imply that Pitcher had benefited from access to the original manuscripts.

In the nineteenth century the original Erskine edition was reissued numerous times, especially in Edinburgh and Worcester, Massachusetts. Both the Religious Tract Society (London) and the American Tract Society (New York) also kept it available in print. The Pitcher edition was reissued twice in London. Beyond this, of course, *A History of the Work of Redemption* was a standard part of the various collected editions of Edwards' works, beginning with that issued at Leeds in 1806–1811 (8 vols.). The most important collection came out at Worcester in 1808, and numerous others followed.

Finally, *A History of the Work of Redemption* was translated. It was brought out almost immediately in Dutch at Utrecht (1776). In the nineteenth century it was issued twice in Welsh (at Bala in 1829; later, undated, from New York, by the American Tract Society). A translation into French was published at Toulouse in 1854, and one into Arabic at Beirut in 1868. Without question *A History of the Work of Redemption* proved to be one of the most widely distributed of Jonathan Edwards' writings. No doubt its greatest influence was in the popular culture as a "historical" construction of evangelical consciousness rather than as a strictly philosophical or theological treatise like *Religious Affections* or *Freedom of the Will*. In this sense it informed

<!-- p. 028 -->

the nineteenth-century evangelical understanding of the world and served as a framework within which progressive refinement of theories of dispensations took place.

### 2. Redemption as God's Greatest Work

#### Redemption As A Theological Preoccupation In The New England Puritan Tradition

Redemption was a fundamental theme in New England Puritan thought from its beginnings. Thomas Hooker's writings exemplify this preoccupation in his early published sermons.[^002-note61] This venerable patriarch had been a leader in the migration from old England in the 1630s, and also in the subsequent departure of a small group that removed to the Connecticut River Valley from the Massachusetts Bay patent. Modern critical scholarship has but followed him in confirming the centrality of redemption by emphasizing the questions of "visible sainthood" and "preparation for salvation." Jonathan Edwards' initial publication took redemption as its topic: *God Glorified in the Work of Redemption*, *by the Greatness of Man's Dependence upon Him*, *in the whole of It* was preached as a public lecture in Boston in 1731.[^002-note62] A brief review of his "Miscellanies" has indicated that he repeatedly returned to the subject throughout his life, but especially in the early years of his maturity, at Northampton. His composition of thirty sermons as "A History of the Work of Redemption" was entirely congruent with the broader tradition in which he stood, and it was also the development of a theme already central in his own work.

What is noteworthy about the Redemption Discourse is not so much the subject but the approach to it which Edwards chose to develop. Earlier tradition was largely given to close analysis of the "application of redemption"—the phrase was used by Hooker—in the soul of the Christian.[^002-note63] The great theological doctrines of the incarnation of the divine as human in Jesus as the Christ and the Savior's atonement for human sin so as to achieve salvation for the faithful were taken for granted in this literature. The center of concern was how this

<!-- p. 029 -->

objective given of the spiritual economy might be rendered real in the lives of the individual saints who were its subjects—the application of redemption translated into a concern for the morphology of conversion and became a preoccupation with visible sainthood.[^002-note64] It entailed a scrupulous analysis of the steps to salvation, especially in the lives of individual saints, but not excluding salvation's collective expression.[^002-note65]

These interests substantially overlapped with those of the adherents of Pietism, which developed in Continental circles in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.[^002-note66] The Pietists were deeply influenced by English Puritanism's concern with the application of redemption. And a mutual interest continued on the part of German-speaking Pietists and English-speaking Puritans throughout the seventeenth and into the eighteenth centuries. These traditions interpenetrated in the middle Colonies of the New World in Edwards' lifetime, and this circumstance must be seen as background to the Great Awakening in that region.[^002-note67] What distinguished these cognate traditions was their respective emphases and focuses. The Puritan tradition initially developed and nurtured the Reformed commitment to renovate the common life as a whole as well as individual Christians and their purified churches; the Pietist tradition carried forward a more typically Lutheran attitude of greater indifference toward the social and political context within which redeemed individuals and their religious groupings lived.

The side of the Puritan tradition concerned with the application of redemption and visible sainthood continues strongly in Edwards. In his revival preaching he was preeminently the skilled "doctor of salvation," simultaneously holding forth the possibility of redemption and the terror of everlasting damnation. Thus "Sinners in the Hands

<!-- p. 030 -->

of an Angry God" deserves the attention it has received as an exemplar of his preaching.[^002-note68] But it was preaching of one particular kind—that directed to securing the redeemed in their faith through holding forth with exceptional vigor the dreadful alternative to it. He also took a vital interest in the application of redemption, and this theme stands behind the 1734 awakening chronicled in his *Faithful Narrative*, as well as behind the Great Awakening. His reflections issued in a series of increasingly discriminating analyses of the spiritual life, culminating in the masterful treatise *Religious Affections*.[^002-note69] Here the full range of Edwards' analytic skills was marshaled to review the experience of the subjects of redemption.

The application of redemption provided the focus for much of Edwards' mature career. For example, the energy he devoted to that ambitious transatlantic revival movement, the Concert of Prayer, was precisely the direct outcome of his concern, although it also showed his continuing sense of (and clearly enhanced appreciation for) the connection between the New England and at least the Scottish traditions.[^002-note70] In addition, he seems to have been aware of the Continental Pietism of Spener at Halle and the role of Zinzendorf in both Europe and the Middle Colonies. Another example is his reversal of Stoddard's relatively open position on membership in the church, a direct expression of Edwards' continuing conviction that "closing with salvation" was a matter of utmost urgency. It is imperative to insist, however, that while he focused great energies on the application of redemption, he did not make the transition in his own work that would come about in the next century. This was an increasing preoccupation among Romantics with redemption viewed subjectively.[^002-note71]

Within the tradition of nineteenth-century religious thought in America reaching from Edwards, this transition or turn can be perceived

<!-- p. 031 -->

developing in both orthodox and heterodox ways. The thought of a Horace Bushnell, to take the first case, has developed far toward a modern position that since language as a cultural product is the medium in which religious claims are made, any religious claims advanced are necessarily rooted in the human subject.[^002-note72] While Bushnell remained committed to the comprehensive and traditional Christian confession, for him it was essentially just that—a compelling description of the phenomenal world, not a secure disclosure of the noumenal realm. On the other side, Ralph Waldo Emerson was no less preoccupied with redemption in the experience of its subjects. But for him the traditional Christian symbols were equated with, or reduced to, symbols derived from nature, and the life of the spirit was construed in thoroughly heterodox terms.[^002-note73] But for us the central issue is that Edwards' concern with redemption represented his appropriation of central elements of the New England religious tradition that would, in turn, be developed further by others.

As important as it is to observe that Edwards' concern for redemption as the most basic religious category was carrying forward a prominent strand of New England culture, we must note that he also turned these concerns in a different direction entirely. Here he proposed systematic attention to the "objective" side of the issue: redemption seen in relationship to the whole of creation as the means to comprehend the relationship of the world to God. His continuing reflection on these questions led him to carry the question even further back, into conjecture that the human understanding of the Work of Redemption established the nature of the Godhead as irreducibly trinitarian. The late essay "The End for Which God Created the World," posthumously published in *Two Dissertations*, addressed the question of the limits of human understanding of redemption.[^002-note74] But it was already an implicit issue in the Redemption Discourse, though not as fully developed. As has been suggested, the "Miscellanies" show its presence even earlier. In effect, Edwards' argument was, so to speak, that if creation is a stage, the purpose of which is to permit

<!-- p. 032 -->

the drama of redemption to be played out, the outcome of the drama (and thus the reason for creation) is God's self-glorification. He does not agonize at length over *why* the created world exists, for its purpose is to effect the redemption of mankind, the objective side of the process so thoroughly inquired into on its subjective side both in the tradition in which Edwards stood and in his own work. A framework such as this suggests why his "history" of the Work of Redemption was so central to his intellectual life and how he approached this major project. It also helps to explain why he always intended it to be a summary theological statement.

Edwards defined the Work of Redemption as taking place between "the fall of man and the end of the world," or last judgment.[^002-note75] The series of events constituting this "history" properly was given in narrative or dramatic terms. But although his project depended profoundly on the Bible and grew out of it, we should not suppose that Edwards' sources for his discussion were confined to it. It is also wrong to suppose that his efforts are to be understood as an exercise in bibliolatry. For him, the Scripture offered an incomplete and complex presentation of the "history," and, moreover, the scriptural version could be easily misread. At the same time, Scripture provided accounts of events that Edwards thought critical in God's Work of Redemption. Examples are the redemption of Israel out of Egypt and the securing of David's kingship over Israel. Edwards augmented the incomplete "historical" sections with Scripture prophecy, in and through which the narrative account of the redemptive scheme was interpreted and fleshed out. This gave him not only a correct understanding of events narrated in Scripture history, but also permitted interpretation of events that transpired outside its purview (examples being the significance of the rise of the Roman empire and the contribution classical pagan philosophy made to the scheme of redemption). Prophecy also disclosed events yet to come that would complete God's Work of Redemption (the destruction of Antichrist and the last judgment). So although there is a sense in which the "history" of the Work of Redemption depends upon the Scriptures and certainly could not be comprehended by humans without them, the Scriptures do not contain its entirety. Indeed, the Scriptures might be said to have as their divine purpose or intention the work itself.

<!-- p. 033 -->

It is crucial to identify precisely the social location and the nature of the account of God's Work of Redemption which Edwards finally created. His "history" is addressed to a community which is potentially redeemed, as an exhortation to its members to be saved, to "close with salvation." These sermon-discourses seek to engage their hearers and readers. If creation is the stage and God's Work of Redemption the drama being played out upon it, Scripture is the established text of what has taken place in the drama and the partial text of what is to come. To continue the analogy, Edwards is part aspiring producer, part theater critic. His sermon hearers and treatise readers are at once unwittingly acting, attending the performance, devouring reviews, and yearning for consummation of the project. This analogy, like all analogies, breaks down at this point, and such a comparison with the stage might in any case have struck Edwards as at best frivolous and at worst blasphemous. But it does help to suggest to the modern critical reader the complex relationships between Godhead, Scripture, redemption, Edwards' text, the hearers, and finally the readers that his project comprises. We must focus on the text of the Redemption Discourse to understand what makes it so effective, while recognizing that Edwards' preaching of his "history" was part exposition of the Work of Redemption, part production of its story, and part critical commentary upon it.

To analyze the Redemption Discourse, appreciation for the sermon form is crucial. Beyond extensive attention to this question we will make and emphasize a distinction between, on the one hand, the narrative base of the text (which recounts events in serial order) and, on the other, various levels of meaning invoked to interpret events that took place in biblical times, have taken place since then, or are yet to take place, in relationship to the redemptive process. It is important to emphasize that events in this narrative base already carry an interpretation—these are not neutral occurrences, now available for the first time. Rather, these occurrences are already very familiar, and their significance is established, like the rescue of one righteous man and his family from a flood so that they can be bearers of salvation, or the release of a people under captivity in Babylon, or the fall of Jerusalem before the might of Rome, or the embrace of Christianity by an empire. These events are basic themes already established, but in their perfection, the whole is enriched by skillful anticipation of later themes and extensive elaboration of earlier ones as the consummation of all things approaches. Like the playing of a

<!-- p. 034 -->

piece of music or the production of a play for that matter, the whole adds up to so much more than the parts taken in isolation.

Edwards' devices for inventing meanings or elaborating interconnections were relatively conventional. In effect, he availed himself of a series of literary strategies which involved claims about the revelatory power of isolated units in the narrative base. The strongest claim is the assertion that at several points Christ actually appeared to Israel before his incarnation. Slightly less strong claims concern a much broader class of materials: prophecies. A weaker level of claim, still very important, is made by typology. Here the individual or event is a figure that, while retaining its own integrity in the narrative base, yet discloses another reality. As we shall see, Edwards uses this method fully, but he feels free to apply typology less rigorously as well. Still weaker forms of elaboration of the basic narrative account occur in claims concerning images or shadows of fundamental reality.

To move into a systematic analysis of Edwards' literary strategies necessarily misrepresents them, because it treats as separate elements that are fused in his text. But it ought to be evident that, already in the thirty sermons preached in 1739, he had moved far toward the conception of a treatise or sustained essay on the fundamentals of the Christian religion, which he would organize in terms of the objective side of the redemptive process, namely, God's Work of Redemption. The sermons stand without the ambitious development he intended for them. But they stand also as a literary achievement in their own right, without the revision, refinement, and extension he would have given them.

#### The Redemption Discourse And The Transformation Of The Sermon Form

While Jonathan Edwards worked within the traditional structure of the sermon, he was also engaged in transforming it. Sermon series, like "Charity and Its Fruits" preached the preceding year, were traditionally developed around the exegesis of a series of verses, a scriptural chapter, or even a whole biblical book. The preaching unit was defined through the rhetorical conventions of the Puritan tradition. A scriptural text, a verse (or part thereof) was explicated so as to develop it in relation to its setting and to clarify it in terms of content. Then a doctrine or rational statement of the principle conveyed through the text was enunciated. The sermon developed "observations" or "reasons," that is, rational elaborations of the doctrine,

<!-- p. 035 -->

drawing upon a range of sources both within the tradition and outside it. References to classical authors were included, as well as historical precedents, allusions to current events, and commonsense observations. This served as the core of the sermon. Finally, the implications of the whole for the auditors were pointed out; the sermon was "improved" for their benefit. This marvelously efficient instrument provided a framework within which the preacher could suit his delivery to circumstance and develop variations as warranted by occasion. Its tripartite structure suggested the conventional threefold psychological model in which human nature was thought to involve reason, will, and emotions.[^002-note76] In making use of this form, Edwards was simply appropriating a recognized tradition that had proved effective since evolving to roughly this stage among Puritans in the late Elizabethan years.[^002-note77]

Edwards explicitly framed the Redemption Discourse using these basic elements of text, doctrine, and application or improvement. He did not isolate a distinct section of "reasons," although three "propositions" or specifications of the doctrine guided the development of the whole. His rather full explication of the doctrine in Sermon One, after he had briefly introduced the text, may indicate that the conventional structure had undergone a modification in which rational elaboration was drawn into and conflated with text and doctrine. Where this occurs, some have proposed, we have an adaptation of the rhetorical form that indicates a significant change in assumptions about human psychology.[^002-note78] That may certainly be an important insight into Edwards as preacher and a significant aspect of the Great Awakening

<!-- p. 036 -->

in American culture. At least with respect to the Redemption Discourse, however, it is more important to view the substantial part of these thirty sermons—that not explicitly devoted to text, doctrine, or application—as an elaboration of the rational content that makes it the central argument of the whole. In this framework, the "history" of the Work of Redemption precisely fulfilled the role conventionally played by "reasons" in Puritan preaching: sustained and compelling arguments for the doctrine adduced from Scripture and redemptive events, assembled as authoritative and directed to the will. According to this interpretation, Edwards was developing the sermon structure to the point at which the central core of rational argumentation was virtually a treatise in its own right, though of course he would introduce it by text and doctrine and conclude it by improvement.

We have noted that Edwards' text and doctrine are both fully explicated in the course of the first of the thirty sermons. Thereafter he devotes eleven preaching occasions to a close discussion of the dispensations through which redemption was advanced from the fall of man to the coming of Christ. This development of God's Work of Redemption takes place under the general text and doctrine, with additional "observations" about the last dispensation.
