Their self-righteousness does, in effect, charge Christ's offering up himself in these sufferings as the greatest instance of folly that ever men or angels saw, instead of being the most glorious display of divine wisdom and grace that ever was seen. Yea, self-righteousness makes all that Christ did through the whole course of his life, and all that he said and suffered for through that whole time, and his incarnation itself, and not only so, but all that God had been doing in the great dispensations of his providence from the beginning of the world to that time, as all nothing but a scene of the most wild,[^004-note1156] and extreme, and transcendent folly.

Is it any wonder then that a self-righteous spirit is so represented

<!-- p. 338 -->

in Scripture, and spoken of as that which is most fatal to the souls of men. And is it any wonder that God is represented in Scripture as being so provoked with the Pharisees, and others that trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and were proud of their goodness, and thought that their own performances were a valuable price of God's favor and love. Let persons hence be warned against a self righteous spirit. You that are seeking your salvation and taking pains in religion, if there are any such here present, take heed to yourselves that you don't trust in what you do: That you don't harbor any such thoughts that God now seeing how you are reformed, how you take pains in religion, and how you are sometimes affected, will be pacified towards you with respect to your sins; And on the account of it will not be so angry for your former sins[^004-note1157] and that you shall gain on him by such things, and draw his heart to show you mercy. Or at least that God ought to accept of what you do, so as to be inclined by it in some measure to forgive you and have mercy on you. If you entertain this thought, that God is obliged to it and don't do justly if he refuse to regard your prayers and pains, and so quarrel with God and complain of it for not doing it, this shows what your opinion is of your own righteousness, viz. that 'tis a valuable price of salvation and ought to be accepted of God as such. Such complaining of God and quarreling with him for not taking more notice of your religion, plainly shows that [you] are guilty of all that arrogance that has been spoken of, thinking yourself sufficient to offer the price of your own salvation.

*Thirdly*.[^004-note1158] What has been said on this subject affords matter of reproof to those that carelessly neglect the salvation of Christ, such who live a senseless kind of life, neglecting[^004-note1159] their business of religion and their own precious souls for the present, not taking any course to get an interest in Christ, or what he has done and suffered, or any part in that glorious salvation he has purchased by that price; but rather have their minds taken up about the gains of the world or about the vanities and pleasures of youth. And make so light of what they hear from time to time of Christ's salvation that they for the present don't so much as seek after it. Let me here apply myself to you in some expostulatory interrogations.

<!-- p. 339 -->

1.[^004-note1160] Shall so many prophets, and kings, and righteous [men] have their minds so much taken up with the prospect of the purchase of salvation being wrought out in ages long after their death, and will you so neglect it when actually accomplished? You have heard what great account the church of God in all ages made of the future redemption of Christ; how joyfully they expected it, how they spoke of it, how they studied and searched[^004-note1161] into these things, how they sung joyful songs about, and had their hearts greatly engaged about it and yet never expected to see it done, did not expect that it would be accomplished till many ages after their death, 1 Peter 1:10–12 ["Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently, … what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, … the sufferings of Christ.… Which are now reported unto you"]. How much did Isaiah, and Daniel, and other prophets speak ‹concerning this redemption›. How was David's mind taken [up; he] declared all his salvation, 2 Samuel 23:5.[^004-note1162] How much did he employ his voice and harp,[^004-note1163] though they beheld it as yet accomplished, and it was to be so long a time. And before that, how did Abraham and other patriarchs rejoice; and even the saints before the flood, though so long future and so very faintly and obscurely revealed.

Now these things are declared to you as[^004-note1164] actually fulfilled. The church now has seen all accomplished, all those great things they so joyfully prophesied of, and you are abundantly shown how those things were accomplished, Matthew 13:17, "Verily I say unto you, many prophets.…"[^004-note1165] And yet when these things are thus abundantly set before you as already accomplished, how do you slight them, how light do you make of them, how little are they taken notice of by you, how unconcerned about them, following other things and not so much as feeling any interest in them. Indeed, your sin is extremely aggravated in the sight of God. God has put you under very great advantages for your eternal salvation, far greater than those saints of old enjoyed, under a more glorious dispensation, [with] a more clear revelation of Christ and his salvation.[^004-note1166]

<!-- p. 340 -->

2.[^004-note1167] Shall the angels be so engaged about this salvation of Christ ever since the fall of man, though they are not immediately concerned, and will you who need it and have it offered to you be so careless about it[^004-note1168] You have heard how the angels at first were subjected to Christ as mediator, and how they have all along been ministering spirits to him in this affair. They have in all the great dispensations you have heard of, from the beginning of the world, been active and as a flame of fire in this affair, being most diligently employed as ministering spirits to minister to Christ in this great affair of man's redemption. And when Christ came, how engaged were their minds. [They] came to Zacharias, and came to Mary, to Joseph.[^004-note1169] And how were their minds engaged in the time of the birth of Christ; whole multitude of heavenly hosts sang, and from time to time ministered to Christ when on earth: [at the] time of his temptation, [in his] agony, at his resurrection, [and at his] ascension. All things show that they were greatly engaged, and the Scripture informs us they pry into these things, 1 Peter 1:12, "Which things the angels [desire to look into]." And how are they represented in the Revelation[^004-note1170] as being employed in heaven in singing.[^004-note1171] Shall these take so much notice who don't need [it], have no immediate concern or interest in it, or offer of it; and shall you to whom it is offered—for [you] are in such extreme necessity—‹neglect and take no notice of it›?

3.[^004-note1172] Was it worth the while for Christ to labor so hard, and do and suffer so much, to procure this salvation; and is [it] not worth the while for you to be at some labor in seeking of it? Was it a thing of so great importance that salvation should be procured for sinners, as that it was worthy to lie with such weight on the mind of Christ as to induce him to ‹suffer even death itself›? Though he stood in need of nothing, though he was like to gain nothing of addition to his eternal happiness, get nothing by those that he saves, did not need 'em; was it of such importance that sinners should be saved that he might properly be induced to ‹submit to such humiliation and suffering›.

<!-- p. 341 -->

And yet [is] it not worth the while for you[^004-note1173] who are one of those miserable sinners that need this salvation and must perish eternally without [it], to take earnest pains to obtain an interest in it after it is procured and all things are ready?

4.[^004-note1174] Shall the great God be so concerned about this salvation as so often to overturn the world to make way for it, and when all is done is it not worth your seeking after? How has the Lord of heaven and earth been, as it were, engaged about this affair; what great, what wonderful things has he done from one age to another, removing kings and setting up kings, raising up a great number of prophets, separating a distinct nation from the rest of the world, overturning one nation and kingdom and another, and often overturning the state of the world, and so continue bringing one change and revolution after another for forty centuries, or hundreds of years in succession, to make way? And when he has done all, and at the close of these ages, the great savior comes: and[^004-note1175] becoming incarnate, and passing through a long series of reproaches and suffering, and then suffering all the waves and billows of God's wrath for men's sin as they enveloped[^004-note1176] and passed over his soul; after all, is it not worthy of your taking so much notice of or being so much concerned about, though you are one of those persons that need this salvation; but that it should be thrown by and made nothing of in comparison of worldly gain, or gay clothing, or youthful diversions, and other such trifling things?

O that you that live negligent of this salvation would consider what you do; what you have had from this subject may show you what reason there is in that of the Apostle, Hebrews 2:3, "How shall we escape, if we neglect [so great salvation]." And in that Acts 13:41, "Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish." God looks on such as you as great enemies of the cross of Christ, and adversaries and despisers of all the glory of this great work. And if God[^004-note1177] has made such account of the glory of salvation as to destroy many nations, and so often to overturn all nations, to prepare the way for the glory to his Son in this affair, how little account will he make of the lives and souls of ten thousand such opposers and despisers as you, that continue impenitent

<!-- p. 342 -->

in comparison of that glory. When he shall hereafter come and find that your welfare stands in the way of that glory, why surely you shall be dashed in pieces, as a potter's vessel, and trodden down as the mire of the streets.[^004-note1178] God may through wonderful patience bear with wicked, careless sinners for a while, but he will [not long] bear with such despisers of his dear Son and his great salvation, the glory of which he has had so much at heart, before he will utterly consume them without remedy or mercy.

[^004-note1179]I will conclude with a second use of encouragement to burdened souls very briefly to put their trust in Christ for salvation. To all such as are not careless and negligent, but do make[^004-note1180] seeking an interest in Christ their main business, being sensible in some measure of their necessity of an interest, being afraid of the wrath to come; to such, what has been said on this subject holds forth great matter of encouragement to come and venture their souls in the Lord Jesus Christ. Here consider two things in particular.

1.[^004-note1181] The completeness of the purchase that has been made. As you have heard, this work of purchasing salvation was wholly finished during the time [of Christ's humiliation].[^004-note1182] So here is need of nothing more: the servants are now sent forth with the message which we have account of in Matthew 22:4 ["Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage"]. Are your sins many and great, here is enough.[^004-note1183] There is no need of any righteousness of yours; come freely without money and without price; come naked; come as a poor condemned [sinner]; come cast yourself down at Jesus' feet, as one just condemned and most utterly helpless. Here is complete salvation.

2.[^004-note1184] For Christ to reject one that thus comes to him would be to frustrate all those great things that you have heard of, that God had wrought from the fall of man, all that Christ did and suffered: Christ's incarnation, all the great things done in preparation, for all was for that end, that those might be saved that come to Jesus. Therefore you may be sure Christ will not be backward; he don't desire to

<!-- p. 343 -->

frustrate himself in his own work, it[^004-note1185] cost him too dear for that. God the Father won't refuse you, for he don't desire to frustrate himself in all that he did for so many hundreds and thousands of years. Come therefore, hearken to the sweet and earnest calls of Christ to your soul. Do as he invites, and as he commands you in Matthew 11:28–30, "Come unto me, all [ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest]. Take my yoke [upon you, and learn of me, … and ye shall find rest unto your souls]. For my yoke is easy, [and my burden is light]."[^004-note1186]

<!-- p. 344 -->

### No. 7: SERMON EIGHTEEN

[^004-note1187]

[^004-note1188]

> *[For the moth shall eat them up like a garment*, *and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever*, *and my salvation form generation to generation.]*

Isaiah 51:8

#### DOCTRINE

> *[The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.]*

[^004-note1189]WE are come now to the third and last period of this whole space of time beginning with Christ's resurrection, and reaching to the end of the world, and would now show how the Work of Redemption was also carried on through this period from this proposition, that the space of time from the end of Christ's humiliation to the end of the world is all taken up in bringing about the great effect or success of Christ's purchase.

Not but that there were not great effects and glorious successes of Christ's purchase of redemption before, even from the beginning of the generations of men. But all that success of Christ's redemption that was before, was only preparatory and was by way of anticipation, as some few fruits are gathered before the harvest. There was no more success before Christ came than God saw needful to prepare the way for his coming.[^004-note1190] The proper time of the success or effect of Christ's purchase of redemption is after the purchase has been made; as the proper time for the world to enjoy the light of the sun is the day time after the sun is risen, though it may be that some small

<!-- p. 345 -->

matter of it [is] reflected from the moon and planets before.[^004-note1191] And even the success of Christ's redemption while he himself was on earth was very small in comparison of what it was after the conclusion of the period of his humiliation. But Christ's having finished that greatest and most difficult of all works, the work of the purchase of redemption, now is come the time for obtaining the end of it and obtaining the glorious effect of it. This is the next work he goes about. Having gone through the whole course of his sufferings and humiliation, there is an end to all things of that nature; he is never to suffer[^004-note1192] any more, but now is the time for him to obtain the joy that was set before him.[^004-note1193] Having made his soul an offering for sin, now is the time for him to see his seed and to have a portion divided to him with the great and to divide the spoil with the strong.[^004-note1194]

This is pointed out by the Scripture. One design of Christ in what he had done in his humiliation was to lay a foundation for the overthrow of Satan's kingdom; and now is come the time to effect it, as Christ a little before his crucifixion said, John 12:31, "Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out." Another design was to gather together in one all things in Christ; now is come the time for this also, John 12:32, "And I, if I be lifted up … will draw all men unto me," which is agreeable to Jacob's prophecy of Christ that when "Shiloh come; to him should the gathering of the people be," Genesis 49:10.[^004-note1195] Another design is the salvation of the elect; now when his sufferings are finished and his humiliation is perfected, is come the time for that also, Hebrews 5:8–9, "Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things that he suffered; And being made perfect, he became[^004-note1196] the author of eternal salvation to all them that obey him." Another design was to accomplish by these things great glory to the persons of the Trinity; now also is come the time for that, John 17:1, "Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also [may glorify thee]." Another design is the glory of the saints; now is [come the time for that also,

<!-- p. 346 -->

John 17:2],[^004-note1197] "As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him." And all the dispensations of God's providence henceforward, even to the final consummation of all things, is to give Christ his reward, and fulfill his end in what he did and suffered upon earth, and to fulfill the joy that was set before him.[^004-note1198]

[^004-note1199]Here before I enter on the consideration of any particular things accomplished in this period, I would briefly observe some things in general concerning this period, and particularly how the times of this period are represented in Scripture.

1.[^004-note1200] The times of this period for the most part are those which in the Old Testament are called the latter days. We often in the prophets of the Old Testament read of such and such things that should come to pass[^004-note1201] "in the latter days" and sometimes "in the last days."[^004-note1202] Now these expressions in the prophets are most commonly to be understood of the times of this period that we are now upon.[^004-note1203] They are called the latter days and the last days because this is the last period of the series of God's providences on earth, the last period of that great work of providence, the Work of Redemption, which is as it were, the sum of all God's works of providence, the time wherein the church is under the last dispensation of the covenant of grace that ever it will be under on earth.

2.[^004-note1204] The whole time of this period is sometimes in Scripture called, the end of the world, as 1 Corinthians 10:11, "Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come." And the Apostle in the Hebrews 9:26 in this expression of "the end of the world" means the whole of the gospel day, from the birth of Christ to the finishing of the day of judgment, "But now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself."[^004-note1205] This space of time may well be called the end

<!-- p. 347 -->

of the world, for this whole time is taken up in bringing things to their great end and issue, to that great issue that God had been preparing the way for in all the great dispensations of providence form the first fall of man to this time. Before things were in a kind of preparatory state, but now they are in a finishing state. 'Tis the winding up of things that is all this while accomplishing. An end is now brought to the former carnal worldly state of things, which by degrees vanishes, and a spiritual state begins to be established, and so to be established more and more. First an end is brought to the former state of the church, which may be called its worldly state, the state wherein it was subject to carnal ordinances and the rudiments of the world. And then an end is brought to the Jewish state in the destruction of their city and country. And then after that an end is brought to the old heathen empire in Constantine's time, which is another and further degree of the winding up and finishing of the world. And the next step is finishing[^004-note1206] Satan's visible kingdom in the world, upon the fall of Antichrist and the calling of the Jews. And last will come the destruction of the outward frame of the world itself, at the conclusion of the day of judgment.

But the world is all this while, as it were, a-finishing, though it comes [to] an end by several steps and degrees. Heaven and earth began to shake in order to a dissolution, according to the prophecy of Haggai before Christ came, that so only those things that cannot be shaken may remain, i.e. that those things that are to come to an end may come to end, and that only those things may remain that are to remain to all eternity.[^004-note1207] So in the first place the carnal ordinances of the Jewish worship came to an end, to make way for the establishment of that spiritual worship, the worship of the heart that is to endure to all eternity; John 4:21, "Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when [ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father]"; John 4:23, "But the hour cometh, [and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him]"—which is one instance of the temporary world's coming to an end and the eternal world's beginning. And then after that the outward temple and the outward city Jerusalem came to an end, to give place to the setting up of the spiritual[^004-note1208] temple and the spiritual city

<!-- p. 348 -->

which are to last to eternity—which is another instance of removing those things that are ready to vanish away, that those that cannot be shaken may remain. And then after that the old heathen Roman empire comes to an end to make way for the empire of Christ which shall last to all eternity—which [is] another step of bringing the temporal world to an end, the beginning of the world to come, which is an eternal world. And then after that, upon the fall of Antichrist, end is put to Satan's visible kingdom on earth to establish Christ's kingdom which shall last to all eternity, as the prophet Daniel says, Daniel 7:27, "And the kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven, shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him"—which is another instance. And then lastly the very frame of this corruptible world shall come to an end, to make way for the church to dwell in another dwelling place that shall last to all eternity—which is the last instance.

[^004-note1209]The world's thus, as it were, coming to end by various steps and degrees is perhaps the reason why the Apostle says that the "ends of the world" are come on us; not the end but the ends, of the plural number, as though the world has several endings one after another. The gospel dispensation is the last state of things in the world, and this state is a finishing state; it is all spent in finishing things off that had before been preparing, or abolishing temporal things that had before stood. It is all spent, as it were, in summing things up and bringing them to their issue and their proper fulfillment. Now all the old types are fulfilled, and all the prophecies of all the prophets from the beginning of the world shall have been fulfilled in this period.

3.[^004-note1210] That state of things that is attained in the events of this period is called "a new heaven and a new earth."

> Isaiah 65:17–18 ["For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind. But be ye glad and rejoice for ever in that which I create: for, behold, I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy"], Isaiah 66:22 ["For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith the Lord, so shall your seed and your name remain"],

<!-- p. 349 -->

 Isaiah 51:16 ["And I have put my words in thy mouth, and I have covered thee in the shadow of mine hand, that I may plant the heavens, and lay the foundations of the earth."].

[^004-note1211]As the former state of things or the old world by one step after another is through this period coming to an end, so the new state of things or the new world which is a spiritual world is beginning and setting up. The old heaven and earth that are corruptible are shaking, that the new heaven and new earth which cannot be shaken may be established and remain.

In consequence of each of these finishings of the old state of things there is a new day and beginning of a new and eternal state of things. So was that which accompanied the destruction of Jerusalem, which was an establishing the spiritual Jerusalem instead of the literal. So was that, [the destruction of the old heathen empire and all the other endings of the old state of things,][^004-note1212] till at length the very outward form of the old world itself shall come to end, and the church shall dwell in a world new to it, or to a great part of it, even heaven, which will be a new habitation. And then shall be the utmost accomplished that is meant by the new heaven and the new earth, Revelation 21:1.[^004-note1213] The end of God's creating this world was to provide a kingdom for his Son in it; for he is appointed the heir of the world, and that he might have the possession of it and kingdom in it to all eternity. So that so far forth of the kingdom of Christ is set up in the world, so far is the world brought to its end, and the eternal state of things set up. So far are all the great revolutions and changes of the ages of the world brought to their everlasting issue, and all things come to their ultimate period. So far are the waters of the long channel of divine providence, that has so many branches and so many windings and turnings, emptied out and disgorged into their proper ocean that they have been seeking from the beginning and head of their course, and so are come to their rest. So far as Christ's kingdom is established, so far are things wound up and settled in their everlasting state, and a period put to the course of things in this changeable world. So far is the first heavens and the first earth come to an end and the new

<!-- p. 350 -->

heavens and new earth, the everlasting heavens and earth, established in their room.

This leads me to observe,[^004-note1214] 4.[^004-note1215] That that state of things that is attained by the events of this period is what is so often called the kingdom of heaven and kingdom of God. We very often read in the New Testament of "the kingdom of heaven." John the Baptist preached that "the kingdom of heaven was at hand," and so did Christ and his disciples after him,[^004-note1216] referring to something that the Jews in those days expected and very much talked of that they called by that name.[^004-note1217] They seem to have taken their expectation and the name chiefly from that prophecy of Daniel in his interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, Daniel 2:44, "And in the days of these kings shall the Lord[^004-note1218] God of heaven set up a kingdom," together with that in Daniel 7:13–14, ["one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven.… And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom … and his kingdom … shall not be destroyed"].

Now this kingdom of heaven is that evangelical state of things in his church and in the world wherein consists the success of Christ's redemption in this period. There had been other great kingdoms set up before that were earthly kingdoms, as the Babylonian, ‹the Persian, the Grecian, and the Roman monarchies›. But Christ came to set up the last kingdom, which is not an earthly kingdom but an heavenly, and[^004-note1219] so is the kingdom of heaven, John 18:36, "My kingdom is not of this world." This is that kingdom that Christ speaks of, Luke 22:29, "My Father hath appointed to me a kingdom."[^004-note1220] This kingdom began soon after Christ's resurrection, and was accomplished in various steps from that time to the end of the world. Sometimes by "the kingdom of heaven" is meant that spiritual state of the church that began soon after;[^004-note1221] sometimes that glorious, blessed state at the day of judgment, 1 Corinthians 15:50; the Apostle there speaking of the resurrection says, "This I say, that flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God."[^004-note1222]

<!-- p. 351 -->

Under this head I would observe several things particularly for the clearer understanding of what the Scripture says concerning this period.

[^004-note1223]1.[^004-note1224] The setting up the kingdom of Christ is chiefly accomplished by four successive great events, each of which is in Scripture called "Christ's coming in his kingdom." The whole success of Christ's redemption in this is comprehended in one word, viz. his setting up his kingdom. This is chiefly done by four great, successive dispensations of providence, and every one of them is represented in Scripture as Christ's coming.

The first is Christ's appearing in those wonderful dispensations of providence in the apostles' days in setting up the kingdom of Christ and destroying the enemies of his kingdom, which ended in the destruction of Jerusalem. This is called, "Christ coming in his kingdom" in the Matthew 16:28: "Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, that shall not taste of [death] till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom." And so it is represented in the Matthew 24.[^004-note1225]

The second is that which was accomplished in Constantine's time in the destruction of the heathen Roman empire. This is represented as Christ's coming, and is compared to his coming to judgment in the Revelation 6 at the latter end.[^004-note1226] The third is that which is to be accomplished at the destruction of Antichrist. This[^004-note1227] also is represented as Christ's coming in his kingdom in the Daniel 7 and other places, as I may possibly show hereafter when I come to speak of it.[^004-note1228] The fourth and last is his coming to the last judgment, which is the event principally signified in Scripture by Christ's coming in his kingdom.[^004-note1229]

2.[^004-note1230] I would observe that each of the three former of these is a lively image and type of the fourth and last, viz. Christ coming to the final judgment, as the principal dispensations of providence before Christ's final coming were types of kingdoms first coming like it, as Christ's last coming to judgment is accompanied with a resurrection of the

<!-- p. 352 -->

dead, and so is each of the three foregoing with a spiritual resurrection.[^004-note1231] That coming of Christ that ended in the destruction of Jerusalem was preceded with a glorious spiritual resurrection of souls in the calling of the Gentiles and bringing home such multitudes of souls to Christ by the preaching of the gospel. So Christ's coming in Constantine's time was accompanied with a glorious spiritual resurrection of the bigger part of the known world in a restoration of it to a visible church state from a state of heathenism. So Christ coming at the destruction of Antichrist[^004-note1232] [will be attended with a spiritual resurrection][^004-note1233] of the church after it had been long, as it were, dead in the times of Antichrist. This is called the first resurrection in the Revelation 20.[^004-note1234] And as Christ in the last judgment will gloriously manifest himself coming in the glory of his Father, so [in][^004-note1235] each of the three foregoing events Christ gloriously manifests [himself], each one with a gathering together of the elect from the [four winds][^004-note1236] by God's angels with a great sound of a trumpet, Matthew 24:31. As there precedes the last a time of great degeneracy and wickedness,[^004-note1237] so [with the others]. Before each of them a time of great opposition to the church: Before the first by the Jews in their persecutions that we read of in the Acts; before the second, viz. that in Constantine's time, by the heathen; before the third by Antichrist; and before the last, viz. by Gog and Magog.[^004-note1238]

By each of them God delivers his church.[^004-note1239] Each of them is accompanied with a glorious advancement of the state of the church. The first, which ended in the destruction of Jerusalem, was attended with bringing the church into the glorious state of the gospel, a glorious state of the church very much prophesied of of old, whereby the church was advanced into far more glorious circumstances than it was in before under the Jewish dispensation. The second, which was

<!-- p. 353 -->

in Constantine's time, was accompanied with an advancement of the church into a state of liberty from persecution, and the countenance of civil authority, and triumph over their heathen persecutors. The third, which is [at the downfall of Antichrist, will be accompanied with][^004-note1240] the glory of truth and liberty, peace, and joy that have so often [been] told of. The last [will be attended with] advancement to consummate glory in both soul and body in heaven.[^004-note1241] Each of them [is] accompanied with a terrible destruction of the wicked and the church's enemies: first, of the persecuting Jews[^004-note1242] in that amazing destruction [of the temple]; second, dreadful judgments on heathen persecutors of which more [could be told];[^004-note1243] third, Antichrist;[^004-note1244] fourth, on all the ungodly.[^004-note1245] There is [in each] an ending of the old heaven and earth and a beginning of a new; accompanying each an end to a temporal state and a beginning an eternal state.[^004-note1246]

3.[^004-note1247] I would observe that each of those four great dispensations that are represented as Christ's coming in his kingdom[^004-note1248] are but so many steps and degrees of the accomplishment of one event. They aren't the setting up of so many distinct kingdoms of Christ; they are all of them only several degrees of accomplishment of that one event prophesied of in Daniel 7:13–14:

> And I saw in the night [visions], and, behold, one like unto the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And

<!-- p. 354 -->

  there was given [him] dominion, and glory, and a kingdom that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom that which shall[^004-note1249] not be destroyed.[^004-note1250]

This is what the Jews expected and called, "the coming of the kingdom of heaven,"[^004-note1251] and which John the Baptist and Christ had respect to when they said, "the kingdom of heaven is at hand."[^004-note1252] This great event is gradually accomplished, or is accomplished by several steps, those four great events that have been mentioned.

When Christ came with the preaching of the apostles to set up his kingdom in the world, which dispensation ended in the destruction of Jerusalem, then it was accomplished in a glorious degree. When the heathen empire was destroyed in Constantine's time, it was fulfilled in a further degree. When Antichrist [shall be destroyed, it will be accomplished in a yet higher degree].[^004-note1253] When the end of the world is come, then [will it be accomplished] in its most perfect degree of all; then it shall be fully and completely accomplished. And because these four great events are but images one of another and the three former[^004-note1254] but types of the last, and since they are all but only the several steps of the accomplishment of the same thing, hence we find 'em all from time to time prophesied of under one; as they are in the prophecies of Daniel, and as they are in the Matthew 24, where some things seem more applicable to one of them and others to another.[^004-note1255]

4.[^004-note1256] I would observe that as there are several stages of the accomplishment of the kingdom of Christ, so in each one of them the event is accomplished in a further degree than in the foregoing. That in Constantine's time [was] much greater than ‹that which ended in the destruction of Jerusalem›. So that the kingdom of Christ is gradually prevailing and increasing by these several great stages of its fulfillment from the time of Christ's resurrection to the end of the world.

<!-- p. 355 -->

5.[^004-note1257] And lastly it may be observed that the great providences of God between these[^004-note1258] four great events are to make way for the kingdom and glory of Christ in the event following. Those dispensations of providence that were towards the church of God and the world before the destruction of the heathen empire in Constantine's time, seem all to be to make way for the glory of Christ and the happiness of his church in that event. And so the great providences of God that after that till the destruction of Antichrist and the beginning of he glorious times of the church that follow, seem all to be to prepare the way for the greater glory of Christ and his church in that event. And the providences of God that shall be after that to the end of the world, seem to be for the greater manifestation of Christ's glory at the end of the world and in the consummation of all things.

Thus I thought it needful to observe these things in general concerning this last period of the series of God's providences before[^004-note1259] I take notice of the particular providences by which the Work of Redemption is carried on through this period in their order. And before I do that, I must also briefly answer to an inquiry, viz. why the setting up of Christ's kingdom after his humiliation should be so gradual, by so many steps that are so long in accomplishment, when God could easily have finished it at once.[^004-note1260] Though it would be presumption in us to pretend to declare all God's ends in this, yet doubtless much of the wisdom of God may be seen in it by us, and particularly in these two things.

1.[^004-note1261] In this way the glory of God's wisdom in the manner of doing this is more visible to the creature's observation. If it were done at once, in an instant or in a very short time, there would not be opportunity for the creature to perceive and observe all the particular steps of divine wisdom, as when the work is gradually accomplished and one effect of his wisdom is held forth to observation after another. 'Tis wisely determined of God[^004-note1262] to accomplish his great design by a wonderful and long series of events, that the glory of his wisdom may he displayed in the whole series and that the glory of his perfections

<!-- p. 356 -->

may be seen as appearing, as it were, by parts and in particular successive manifestations. For if all that glory that appears in all these events should be manifested at once, it would be too much for us and more than we at once could take notice of; it would dazzle our eyes and be too much for our sight.

2.[^004-note1263] Satan is the more gloriously triumphed over. God could easily by an act of almighty power at once have crushed Satan. But by giving him time to use his utmost subtilty to hinder the success of what Christ had done and suffered, he is not defeated merely by surprise but has large opportunity to ply his[^004-note1264] utmost power and subtilty again and again, to strengthen his own interest all that he can by the work of many ages. Thus God destroys and confounds him, and sets up Christ's kingdom time after time, in spite of all his subtile machination and great works, and by every step to advance it still higher and higher, till at length it is fully set up and Satan perfectly and eternally vanquished in the end of all things.

<!-- p. 357 -->

### SERMON NINETEEN

[^004-note1265]

[^004-note1266]

> *[For the moth shall eat them up like a garment*, *and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever*, *and my salvation from generation to generation.]*

Isaiah 51:8

#### [DOCTRINE]

> *[The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.]*

IN presentation of this subject, viz. the carrying on ‹the Work of Redemption from the fall of man to the end of the world›, we entered in the forenoon on the third and last great period, and on the last proposition, viz. that the space of time from the end of Christ's humiliation to the end of the world was all taken up in accomplishing the success of Christ's purchase.

In the forenoon I observed five things in general concerning this period.

[^004-note1267]I now proceed to take notice of the particular events of it in their order, and 1. I would take notice of those things whereby Christ was put into an immediate capacity for accomplishing the end of his purchase, and 2. show how he obtained and accomplished that success.

First,[^004-note1268] I would take notice of those things by which [Christ] was put into a capacity for accomplishing the end of his purchase. And they are two things, viz. his resurrection and ascension. As we observed before, the incarnation of Christ was necessary in order to Christ's being in a next capacity for the purchase of redemption; so the resurrection

<!-- p. 358 -->

and ascension of Christ were requisite in order to his accomplishing the success of his purchase.

[^004-note1269]1.[^004-note1270] His resurrection. It was necessary in order to Christ's obtaining the end and effect of his purchase of redemption that he should rise from the dead; for God the Father had committed the whole affair of redemption, not only the purchasing of it but the bestowment of the blessings purchased, that he should not only purchase it as priest but actually bring it about as king, and that he should do this as God-man.[^004-note1271] For God the Father would have nothing to do with fallen man in a way of mercy but by a mediator. But in order to Christ's carrying on the Work of Redemption and accomplishing the success of his own purchase as God-man, it was necessary that he should be alive, and so that he should rise from the dead. Therefore Christ, after he had finished this purchase by death and by continuing for a time under the power of death, rises from the dead to fulfill the end of his purchase and himself to bring about that which he died for.[^004-note1272] For this matter God the Father had committed unto him, that he might as Lord of all manage all to his own purposes, Romans 14:9, "For to this end[^004-note1273] Christ both died, and rose, and revived, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living."

Indeed, Christ's resurrection and so his ascension was part of the success of what Christ did and suffered in his humiliation. For though Christ did not properly purchase redemption for himself, yet he purchased eternal life and glory for himself by what he did and suffered, and this eternal life and glory was given him as a reward of what he did and suffered, Philippians 2:8–9, "He humbled himself, [and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross]. Wherefore God also hath highly [exalted him]."[^004-note1274]

And it may be looked upon as part of the success of Christ's purchase if it be considered that Christ did not rise as a private person but as the head of all the elect church; so that they did, as it were, all rise in him. Christ was justified in his resurrection, i.e. God acquitted and discharged him hereby as having done and suffered

<!-- p. 359 -->

enough for the sins of all the elect, Romans 4:25. And he put him in possession of eternal life as the head of the church, as a sure earnest that they should all follow.[^004-note1275] For when Christ rose from the dead, that was the beginning of eternal life in him.[^004-note1276] His life before his death mortal life, a temporal[^004-note1277] life, but his life after his resurrection was an eternal and immortal life, Romans 6:9, "Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death [hath no more, dominion over him]," Revelation 1:18, "I am he that liveth, [and was dead; and, behold I am alive for evermore, Amen]." But he was put in possession of this eternal life as the head of the body, and took possession of it not only to enjoy himself but to bestow [it] on all that believe in him; so that the whole church, as it were, rises in him. And now he that lately suffered so much, after this is to suffer no more forever, but to [have] eternal glory. God the Father neither expects nor desires any more suffering.

This resurrection of Christ is the most joyful event that ever came to pass, because hereby Christ rested from the great and difficult work of purchasing [redemption] and received God's testimony that it was finished. The death of Christ was the greatest and most wonderful event that ever came to pass, but that has a great deal that is sorrowful. But by the resurrection of Christ that sorrow is turned into joy.[^004-note1278] The head of the whole[^004-note1279] church in that event enters on the possession of eternal life, and the whole church is, as it were, "begotten again to a lively hope," 1 Peter 1:3.[^004-note1280] Weeping had continued for a night, but now joy comes in the morning,[^004-note1281] the most joyful morning that ever [was]. This is the day of the reigning of the head of the church, and all the church reigns with him. This is spoken of as a day that was worthy to be commemorated with the greatest joy of all days, Psalms 118:24, "This is the day that God [hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it]."[^004-note1282] And therefore, this above all other days is appointed for the day of the church's spiritual rejoicing to the end of

<!-- p. 360 -->

the world, to be weekly sanctified as their day of holy rest and joy, that the church therein may rest and rejoice with her head.

And as the Genesis 3 is the most sorrowful chapter, so those chapters in the Evangelists that give an account of the resurrection of Christ may be looked upon as the most joyful chapters in all the Bible.[^004-note1283] For those chapters give an account of the finishing of the purchasing of redemption, and the beginning of the glory of the head of the church as the greatest seal and earnest of the eternal glory of all the rest. And it is further to be observed that the gospel day most properly begins with the resurrection of Christ. Till Christ rose from the dead the Old Testament dispensation remained; but now it ceases, all being fulfilled that was shadowed forth in the typical ordinances of that dispensation. So that here most properly is the end of the Old Testament night; and Christ rising from the grave with joy and glory as the joyful bridegroom of the church,[^004-note1284] as a glorious conqueror to subdue their enemies under their feet: or was like the sun rising, as it were, from being under the earth after a long night of darkness, and coming forth as a bridegroom prepared as a strong man to run his race,[^004-note1285] appearing in joyful light to[^004-note1286] enlighten the world. Now that joyful and excellent dispensation begins, that glorious dispensation that the prophets prophesied so much of; now the gospel sun is risen in glory, "and with healing in his wings," that those that fear God's name may "go forth and grow up [as calves of the stall]."[^004-note1287]

2.[^004-note1288] Christ's ascension into heaven. In this I would include his sitting at the right hand of God. For Christ's ascension and sitting at God's right hand can scarcely be looked upon as two distinct things; for Christ's ascension was nothing else but his ascending to God's right, it was his coming to sit down at his Father's right hand in glory.[^004-note1289] This was another thing whereby Christ was put into a capacity for the accomplishing the effect of his purchase, as one that comes to be a deliverer of a people, as their king in order to it, and that he may be

<!-- p. 361 -->

under the best[^004-note1290] capacity for it, is first installed in his throne. We are told that Christ was exalted to this end, that he might accomplish the success of his redemption, Acts 5:31, "Whom he hath exalted with his own right hand to give repentance unto Israel and remission [of sins]."[^004-note1291]

Christ's ascension into heaven was, as it were, his solemn enthronization whereby the Father did set him on the throne, and invest him with the glory of his kingdom that he had purchased for himself, and that he might thereby obtain the success of his redemption in conquering all his enemies, Psalms 110, at beginning, "Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool."[^004-note1292] Christ entered into heaven in order to the obtaining the success of his purchase, as the high priest of old after he had offered sacrifice entered into the holy of holies with the blood of the sacrifice in order to obtain the success of the sacrifice that he had offered, Hebrews 9:12.[^004-note1293] He entered into heaven, there to make intercession for his people, and to plead the sacrifice that he had made in order to the success of it, Hebrews 7:25. And as he ascended into heaven, God the Father did in a visible manner set him on the throne as king of the universe. He then put the angels all under him, and he subjected heaven and earth under him, that he might govern them for the good of the people that he had died for, Ephesians 1:20–22 ["…which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand.… Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion.… And gave him to be the head over all things to the church"].

And as Christ rose from the dead, so he also ascended into heaven as the head of the body and forerunner of all the church; so they, as it were, ascend with him as well as rise with him. So that we are both "raised up together, and made to sit together, in heavenly places in Christ," Ephesians 2:6.[^004-note1294] The day of Christ's ascension into heaven was doubtless a joyful, glorious day in heaven. It was what [can hardly be imagined]; and as heaven received Christ, God-man, to its kingdom, so doubtless it received a great[^004-note1295] accession of glory and happiness far beyond what it had before. So that the times in both parts of the

<!-- p. 362 -->

church, both that part which is in heaven and also that which is on earth, is become more glorious since Christ's humiliation than before.

So much for those things whereby Christ was put into the best capacity for obtaining the success [of redemption]. I now proceed,

II.[^004-note1296] to show how he accomplished that success. And here I would observe that this success[^004-note1297] consists in two things, viz. either in grace or glory. That success that consists in the former of these is to be seen in those works of God that are wrought during those ages of the church wherein the church is continued under the outward means of grace. That success that consists in the latter, viz. glory, has its chief accomplishment as the[^004-note1298] day of judgment. I would,

first,[^004-note1299] consider the former kind of success, consisting in God's grace here, which mainly appears in the works of God during the time that the Christian church continues under means of grace, which is from Christ's resurrection to his appearing in the clouds of heaven to judgment, which includes the three former of those great events of providence before mentioned that are called in Scripture, Christ's coming in his kingdom.[^004-note1300] In speaking of this success I would first, 1. mention those things by which the means of this success were established, and 2. consider the success itself.

1.[^004-note1301] I would consider those dispensations of providence by which the means of this success were established after Christ's resurrection. And here that,

[^004-note1302]1.[^004-note1303] The abolishing of the Jewish dispensation. This indeed was gradually done, but it began from the time of Christ's resurrection in which the abolition of it is founded. This was the first thing done towards bringing the former state of the world to an end. This is to be looked upon as a great means of the success of Christ's redemption, for the Jewish dispensation was not[^004-note1304] fitted for more than one nation; it was not fitted for the practice of the world in general or

<!-- p. 363 -->

for a church of God dwelling in all parts of the world, nor would it have been in any wise practicable by 'em. For when therefore God had a design of enlarging his church, as he did after ‹Christ's resurrection›, it was necessary that this dispensation should be abolished. If it had been continued it would have been a great block and hindrance to [the enlargement of the church].[^004-note1305] And then their ceremonial law by reason of its burdensomeness and great peculiarity of some of its rites was, as it were, a wall of partition—a ground of enmity between the Jews and Gentiles that kept the Gentiles from complying with the true religion. This wall therefore was broken down to make way for the more[^004-note1306] extensive success of the gospel, as Ephesians 2:14–15.

[^004-note1307]2.[^004-note1308] [The second] thing in order [of] time seems to be the appointment of the Christian sabbath, for even though this was gradually established in the Christian church, yet[^004-note1309] those things by which the revelation of God's mind and will was made began on the day of Christ's resurrection, by his appearing then to his disciples,[^004-note1310] and was afterwards confirmed by his appearing from time to time on that day rather than any other day,[^004-note1311] and his sending down the Holy Spirit so remarkably on that day,[^004-note1312] and afterwards in directing that the public assemblies and public worship of Christians should be on that day.[^004-note1313] And so the day of the week on which Christ rose from the dead, that joyful day, is appointed to be the day of the church's holy rejoicing to the end of the world, and the day of their stated public worship. And this is a very great and principal means of the success that the gospel has had in the world.

3.[^004-note1314] The next thing was Christ's appointment of the gospel ministry, and commissioning and sending forth his apostles to teach and baptize all nations. These things were all done under one, as we have an account[^004-note1315] of in Matthew 28, two last verses ["Go ye therefore, and teach

<!-- p. 364 -->

all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world"].

There were three things done by this one instruction and commission of Christ to his apostles, viz.

1.[^004-note1316] The appointment of the office of the gospel ministry. For this commission that Christ gives to his apostles in the most essential parts of it belongs to all ministers, and the apostles by virtue of it were ministers or elders of the church. And they were so by virtue of this commission.

2.[^004-note1317] Here is something peculiar in this commission to the apostles, viz. to go forth from one nation to another preaching the gospel in all the world. The apostles had something above what belonged to their ordinary character as ministers: they had extraordinary power of teaching and ruling that extended to all the churches, and not only all churches that then were but all that should be to the end of the world, by their ministry. And so the apostles were, as it were, in subordination to Christ, made foundations[^004-note1318] of the Christian church: Ephesians 2:20 ["… built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone"]; Revelation 21:14 ["And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb"].

3.[^004-note1319] Here is an appointment of Christian baptism. This ordinance indeed had a beginning before; John the Baptist and Christ ‹both baptized›. But now, especially by this institution, is it established as an ordinance to be upheld in the Christian church to the end of the world. The ordinance of the Lord's supper had been established before.

[^004-note1320]4.[^004-note1321] The next thing to be observed is the enduing the apostles and others with extraordinary and miraculous gifts of the Holy Ghost, such as the gift of tongues, [of healing, of prophecy, etc.].[^004-note1322] The Spirit

<!-- p. 365 -->

of God was poured out in great abundance in this respect. So that not only ministers, but a very great part of the Christians through the world, were endued with them, both old and young, not only officers and more honorable persons but the meaner sort of people, as servants and handmaids, were commonly endued with them, agreeable to Joel's prophecy, Joel 2:28–29 ["… I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy,…also upon the servants and upon the handmaids"]. Which prophecy the apostle Peter takes notice is accomplished in this dispensation, Acts 2:17 ["And it shall come to pass in the last days … I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh"].

How wonderful a dispensation was [this].[^004-note1323] Under the Old Testament but few had such great honor put upon 'em by God. Moses wished [that all the Lord's people were prophets], Numbers 11:29.[^004-note1324] But Joshua thought it much that Eldad[^004-note1325] and Medad [prophesied].[^004-note1326] But now ‹we find the wish of Moses fulfilled›. And this continued in a very considerable degree to the end of the apostolic age, or the first hundred years after the birth of Christ, which is therefore called the age of miracles.

This was a great means of the success of the gospel in that age of establishing the Christian church in all parts of the world, and not only in that age but in all ages to the end of the world. For Christianity being by this means established through so great a part of the known world by miracles, it was after that more easily continued by tradition. And then by means of these extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, the apostles and others were enabled to write the New Testament to be an infallible rule of faith and works and manners to the church to the end of the world. And furthermore these miracles stand recorded in[^004-note1327] those writings as a standing proof and evidence of the truth of the Christian religion to all ages.

5.[^004-note1328] The next thing I would observe is the revealing those glorious doctrines of the gospel fully and plainly, which had under the Old Testament been obscurely revealed. The doctrine of Christ's satisfaction

<!-- p. 366 -->

and righteousness, his ascension and glory, and the way of salvation was under the Old Testament in a great measure hid under the veil of types and shadows and more obscure revelations, as Moses put a veil over his face to hide the shining of it.[^004-note1329] But now the veil of the temple is rent from the top to the bottom[^004-note1330] and Christ, the antitype of Moses, shows the shining of his face without a veil, 2 Corinthians 3:12–13 ["… we use great plainness of speech: and not as Moses, which put a vail over his face"], 2 Corinthians 3:18 ["But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord"]. Now these glorious mysteries are plainly revealed which were in a great measure kept secret from the foundation of the world, Ephesians 3:3–5[^004-note1331] ["… He made known unto me the mystery … whereby … ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men"], Romans 16:25, "According to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since [the world began, but now is made manifest],"[^004-note1332] and Colossians 1:26, "Even the mystery which hath been hid from ages and generations, but now is made manifest to his saints."[^004-note1333]

Thus the sun of righteousness after it is risen from under the earth begins to shine forth clearly, and not only by a dim reflection as it was before. Christ before his death revealed many things more clearly than ever they had been revealed in the Old Testament, but the great mysteries of Christ's redemption and reconciliation by his death, and justification by his righteousness, were not so plainly revealed before[^004-note1334] Christ's resurrection. Christ gave that reason for it, that he would not put new wine [into old bottles],[^004-note1335] and it was gradually done after Christ's resurrection. In all likelihood, Christ much more clearly instructed 'em personally after his resurrection and before his ascension, as we read that he continued with them, Luke 24:45 ["Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures"],

<!-- p. 367 -->

Acts 1:3 ["… He shewed himself alive after his passion … being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God"]. But the clear revelation ‹of these things› was principally after the pouring out of the Spirit the day of Pentecost, agreeable to Christ's promise, John 16:12–13 ["I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now. Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth"]. This clear revelation of the mysteries of the gospel as they are delivered we have chiefly through the hands of the apostle Paul, by whose writings a child may come to know more of the doctrines of the gospel in many respects[^004-note1336] than the greatest prophets knew under the darkness of the Old Testament.

Thus we see how the light of the gospel which began to dawn immediately after the fall, and gradually grew and increased through nil the ages of the Old Testament, as we observed as we went along, is now come to the light of perfect day, and the brightness of the sun shining forth in his unveiled glory.

6.[^004-note1337] The next thing that I would observe is the appointment of the office of deacons in the Christian church, which we have an account of in the Acts 6, to take care for the outward supply of the members of Christ's church, and the exercise of that great Christian virtue of charity, with the greater advantage of which I have lately had occasion to speak to you particularly of.[^004-note1338]

7.[^004-note1339] The calling and qualifying and sending the apostle Paul. This was begun in his conversion, as he was going to Damascus,[^004-note1340] and was one of the greatest means of the success of Christ's redemption that followed.[^004-note1341] For this success was more by the labors, preachings, and writings of this apostle than all the other apostles put together, for as he says, 1 Corinthians 15:10, he "labored more abundantly than they all"; so his success was more abundant than of them all. As he was the apostle of the Gentiles, so it was mainly by his ministry that the Gentiles were called and the gospel spread through the world.[^004-note1342] And our

<!-- p. 368 -->

nation and the other nations of Europe have the gospel among them chiefly through his means; and he is more improved[^004-note1343] in revealing glorious doctrines of the gospel by his writings for the use of the church in all ages than all the other apostles put together.

8.[^004-note1344] The next thing I would observe is the institution of ecclesiastical councils for the heresy controversies and ordering the[^004-note1345] affairs of the church of Christ, of which we have an account in the Acts 15.[^004-note1346]

9.[^004-note1347] The last thing I shall mention under this head is the committing the New Testament to writing. This was all written after Christ's resurrection, and all written either by the apostles or by evangelists that were companions of the apostles. All the New Testament was written by apostles themselves, excepting what was written by Mark and Luke, viz. the Gospels of Mark and Luke, and the book of the Acts of the Apostles. He that wrote the Gospel of Mark is supposed to be he whose mother was Mary, in whose house they were praying for Peter when Peter, brought out of prison by the angel, came and knocked at the door, of which we read, Acts 12:12, "And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying."[^004-note1348] He was companion to the apostles Barnabas and Saul, Acts 15:37, [^004-note1349] "And Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark." He was Barnabas's first cousin, or his sister's son, and seems sometimes to have been a companion of the apostle Paul, Colossians 4:10, "Aristarchus my fellow prisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas, touching whom ye received commandments: If he come unto you receive him." The apostles seem to have made great account of him, as appears by these places and also by Acts 12:25, "And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem, […] and took with [them] John, whose surname was Mark," and Acts 13:5, "And when they were at Salamis, they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews: and they had also John to their minister," and 2 Timothy 4:11, "Only Luke is with me. Take

<!-- p. 369 -->

Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry."

This Luke, who wrote the Gospel of Luke and[^004-note1350] the book of the Acts, was a great companion of the apostle Paul's. He is spoken of as being with him in the last-mentioned place, and speaks of himself as accompanying him in his travails,[^004-note1351] so in his history of the Acts; and therefore he speaks in the first person plural when speaking of Paul's journeys, saying, "We went to such and such a place," "We set sail," "We launched from such a place, and landed at such a place."[^004-note1352] He was greatly beloved by the apostle Paul; he is that beloved physician spoken of, Colossians 4:14. The Apostle ranks Mark and Luke among his fellow laborers in Philemon 24, "Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellow labourers."

The rest of the books were all written by apostles themselves. The books of the New Testament are either historical or doctrinal or prophetical. The historical books are[^004-note1353] the writings of the four Evangelists, giving us the history of Christ, and his purchase of redemption, and resurrection, and ascension; and the Acts of the Apostles, giving an account of the great things by which the Christian church was first established and propagated. The doctrinal books are the epistles. These most of them we have from the great apostle Paul. And we have one prophetical book which takes place after the end of the history of the whole Bible, and gives an account of the great events that were to come to pass, by which the Work of Redemption was to be carried on to the end of the world.

All these books are supposed to have been written before the destruction of Jerusalem, excepting those that were written by the apostle John, who lived the longest of all the apostles, and wrote what he wrote after the destruction of[^004-note1354] Jerusalem, as is supposed. And to this beloved disciple it was that Christ revealed those wonderful things that were to come to pass in his church to the end of time, and he was the person that put the finishing hand to the canon of the Scriptures, and sealed the whole of it. So that now the canon of the Scriptures, that great and standing written rule, that was begun about

<!-- p. 370 -->

Moses' time, is completed and settled and a curse denounced against him that adds anything to it or diminishes anything from it.[^004-note1355] And so all things are established and completed that related to the appointed means of grace. All the stated means of grace were finished in the apostolic age, or before the death of the apostle John, and are to remain unaltered to the day of judgment.

<!-- p. 371 -->

### No. 8: SERMON TWENTY

[^004-note1356]

[^004-note1357]

> *[For the moth shall eat them up like a garment*, *and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever*, *and my salvation from generation to generation.]*

Isaiah 51:8

#### [DOCTRINE]

> *[The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.]*

IN showing from these words how the Work of Redemption was ‹carried on from the fall of man to the end of the world›, after having gone through the two former periods of time into which this whole ‹space› was divided we entered on the last period, even that from the end of Christ's humiliation, and so on the last proposition, viz. that the space of time from ‹Christ's humiliation to the end of the world› was taken up in accomplishing the success and end of Christ's purchase. Under which proposition, after having observed some general things relating to this period, I 1. took notice of those things by which Christ was put into an immediate capacity for accomplishing [these things], viz. his resurrection and ascension, and 2. proposed to show how he obtained or accomplished that success. And here it was observed that this success is obtained either, [1.] in bestowing grace on his elect church, or 2. in bringing the church to glory; and that the success that consists in the former of these is to be seen in those works of God that are wrought during these ages that the church is continued under evil with means[^004-note1358] of grace, and that the latter that consists

<!-- p. 372 -->

in the glory of the church has its chief accomplishment at the day of judgment. And it was proposed to consider each of these differently. And first to consider that success that consists in grace, accomplished from the time ‹of Christ's ascension› to ‹the fall of Antichrist›. In speaking to this, I first took notice of those things by which the means of grace were given and established in the Christian church. And thus far we have gone. And,

II.[^004-note1359] The other thing proposed relating to the success of Christ's redemption during the church's continuance under means of grace was to show how this success was carried on, which is what I would now proceed to do. And here it is worthy to be remembered that the Christian church during its continuance under means of grace is in two very different states, viz.[^004-note1360] 1. in a suffering, afflicted, persecuted state, as for the most part it is from the resurrection of Christ till the fall of Antichrist,[^004-note1361] and 2. [in] a state of peace and prosperity, which is the state that the church for the most part is to be in after the fall of Antichrist. Here,

First,[^004-note1362] I would show how the success of Christ's redemption is carried on during the continuance of the church's suffering state from the resurrection of Christ to the fall of Antichrist. This space of time for the most part is a state of the church's suffering, and is so represented in Scripture. Indeed, God is pleased out of love and pity to his elect to grant many intermissions of the church's suffering during this time whereby these days of tribulation are, as it were, shortened. But from Christ's resurrection till the fall of Antichrist is the appointed day of Zion's troubles. During that space of time for the most part, some part or other of the church is under persecution, and great part of the[^004-note1363] time the whole church, or at least the generality of God's people, have been persecuted.

For the first three hundred years after Christ the church was, for the most part, in a state of great affliction; the object of reproach and persecution, first by the Jews and then by the heathen. After this,

<!-- p. 373 -->

from the beginning of Constantine's time, the church had rest and prosperity for a little while, which is represented in Revelation, [chapter] seven,[^004-note1364] at beginning, by angels holding the four winds for a little while. But presently, after the church again suffered persecution from the Arians and after that, Antichrist arose; and the church was driven away into the wilderness, and was kept down in obscurity and contempt and suffering for a long time under Antichrist before the reformation by Luther and others. And since the Reformation the church's persecutions have been beyond all that ever were before. And though some parts of God's church sometimes has had rest, yet to this day for[^004-note1365] the most part, the true church is very much kept under by its enemies, and some parts of it under grievous persecution. And so we may expect it will continue till the fall of Antichrist, and then will come the appointed day of the church's prosperity on earth, the set time in which God will favor Zion, the time when the saints shall not be kept under by wicked men as it has been hitherto, but wherein they shall be uppermost and "shall reign on earth," as 'tis said, Revelation 5:10, "And [the] kingdom … [shall be] given to the people of the saints,"[^004-note1366] Daniel 7:27.

This suffering state of the church is in Scripture represented as a state of the church's travail, John 16:20–21 ["… ye shall weep and lament.… A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come"]. And Revelation 12:1–2 ["And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun.… And she being with child cried, travailing in birth, and pained to be delivered"]. What the church is in travail striving to bring forth during this time, is that glory and prosperity to the church that shall be after the fall of Antichrist, and then shall she bring forth her child.[^004-note1367] This is a long time of the church's trouble and affliction, and is so spoken of in Scripture, though it be spoken as being but a little season in comparison of the eternal prosperity of the church. Hence the church under the long continuance of this affliction cries out, as in Revelation 6:10, "How long, O Lord, holy and true, [dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth]." And we are told that, "white robes [were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also

<!-- p. 374 -->

and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled]."[^004-note1368] So in the Daniel 12:6, "How long shall it be to the end of these wonders?"

And 'tis to be observed that during this time of the church's suffering, the main instrument of her sufferings has been the Roman government; her afflictions have almost all along been from Rome. That is therefore in the New Testament called Babylon, because as of old the troubles of the city Jerusalem were mainly from that adverse city Babylon; so the troubles of the Christian church, the spiritual Jerusalem,[^004-note1369] during the long time of its tribulation, is mainly from Rome. And all[^004-note1370] before Constantine's time the troubles of the Christian church were from heathen Rome; since then its troubles have been mainly from Antichristian Rome. And as of old the captivity of the Jews ceased on the destruction of Babylon, so the time of the trouble of the Christian church will cease with the destruction of [the] church of Rome, that spiritual Babylon.[^004-note1371]

In showing how the success of Christ's redemption is carried on during this time of the church's tribulation I would, 1. show it was carried on till the destruction of Jerusalem, with which ended the first great dispensation of providence—that is called Christ's coming in his kingdom, and 2. how it was carried on from thence to the destruction of the heathen empire in Constantine's time, which is the second great ‹dispensation of providence, and› 3. how it is carried on from thence to the destruction of Antichrist, when there be wrought the third great dispensation—and with which the days of the church's persecution and travail ends.

[^004-note1372]I.[^004-note1373] I would show how the success of Christ's purchase of redemption was carried on from Christ's resurrection to the destruction of Jerusalem. In speaking of this I would, 1. take notice of the success itself, and 2. the opposition made against it by the enemies of it, and 3. the terrible judgments of God on those enemies.

1.[^004-note1374] I would observe the success itself. Soon after Christ had finished the purchase of redemption and was gone into heaven, and

<!-- p. 375 -->

entered into the holy of holies with his own blood, there began a glorious success and result[^004-note1375] of what he had done and suffered. Having undermined the foundation of Satan's kingdom, his kingdom begins to fall apart. Swiftly did it hasten to ruin in the world, which might well be compared to Satan's "falling like lightning from heaven."[^004-note1376]

Satan before this had exalted his throne very high in the world, even to the very stars of heaven, reigning with great glory in his heathen Roman empire. But never had he before such a downfall as he had soon[^004-note1377] after Christ's ascension. He had, we may suppose, been very lately triumphing in a supposed victory, having brought about the death of Christ which he doubtless gloried in as the greatest feat that ever he did, and probably imagined he had totally defeated God's design by him. But he was quickly made sensible that he had only been ruining his own kingdom when he saw it tumbling so fast so soon after as a consequence of the death of Christ. For Christ by his death having purchased the Holy Spirit, and having ascended and received that Spirit, he poured it forth abundantly for the conversion of thousands and millions of souls. Never had Christ's kingdom been so set up in the world. There probably were more souls converted in the age of the apostles than had been before from the beginning of the world till that time. And thus God so soon begins gloriously to accomplish his promise to his Son, wherein he had promised that he should[^004-note1378] "see his seed," and that the "pleasure [of the Lord shall prosper in his hand]" if he would "make his soul [an offering for sins]." And,

1.[^004-note1379] Here is to [be] observed the success the gospel had among the Jews, for God first began with them. God, being about to reject the main body of that people, first calls in his elect from among them before he forsook them to turn to the Gentiles. It was so in former great and dreadful judgments of God on that nation; the bulk of them were destroyed, and only a remnant saved and reformed. So it was in the rejection of the ten tribes; long before this rejection the bulk of the ten tribes were rejected when they left the true worship of God in Jeroboam's time, and afterwards more fully in Ahab's time,

<!-- p. 376 -->

but yet there was a number of them that God reserved. A number left their possessions in those tribes and went up [and settled in the tribes of Judah and Benjamin].[^004-note1380] And afterwards, there were seven thousand in Ahab's time [who had not bowed the knee to Baal].[^004-note1381] And so in the captivity into Babylon; but a remnant of them returned.[^004-note1382] So now again [the great part of the people were rejected; but some few were saved].[^004-note1383] And therefore the Holy Ghost[^004-note1384] compares this reservation of a number that were converted by the preaching of the apostles to those former remnants, Romans 9:27, "Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel [be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved]."[^004-note1385]
